speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON SINGAPORE COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not possible, in the few minutes which the rules permit me, to describe to the House in more than a summary fashion the Singapore Conference of Commonwealth Heads of Government. With the permission of hon. members, however, I should like to convey to the House some of the impressions that I brought away with me. These impressions, hopefully, will add to the information already received from Singapore in the form of the conference communique and the very full journalistic reports.
The meeting was, as the House is aware, the first regular Commonwealth Conference to take place outside of London, and the first at the head of government level to be sited in Asia. I think that an Asian location was most fortunate, partly because it was in Asia that momentum was first initiated for the Commonwealth to be transformed from its older, more confining structure into the widely representative association which it is today, and partly because an Asian situs permitted conference delegates to live and work in a newly-independ-ent community in which racial harmony is a necessary fact of life. The world, as we know but so often tend to forget in the immediacy of our own domestic problems, is populated to an overwhelming degree by persons who are desperately poor and whose colonial experience in many instances leads them to question the values and the sincerity of the developed countries. All too often as well, "rich" and "white" are regarded by them as synonymous. We forget these facts at our peril.
In Singapore it quickly became apparent that the future of the world will not necessarily be determined in accordance with European conceptions. The Commonwealth, viewed from Singapore, presented challenges to the ingenuity and good will of its members to find ways of communicating across differences measured in many instances by thousands of miles and by centuries of experience, yet without insisting upon adherence to preconceived notions or attitudes. In the result, the value of the Singapore conference might best be described in terms of the comprehension gained by delegates, and not by the persuasion which anyone attempted to exercise.
The conference dealt with a number of important
issues, Mr. Speaker, foremost among them the contentious issue of arms sales to the Republic of South Africa. I am relieved, as I am sure are all here, that, following consideration of factors affecting the security of maritime trade routes, the members agreed to the formation of a committee to study these questions as they relate to the Indian and South Atlantic Oceans in hopes of resolving some of the complex variations and differences of view. I am also pleased that an amended Declaration of Commonwealth Principles, which had been presented earlier to the meeting in its basic form by President Kaunda of Zambia, received the unanimous support of the meeting. Each of these measures confirmed to a large extent the belief by most heads of government that the Commonwealth Association is important; one that is capable of contributing significantly to a better understanding among men of their common ideals and aspirations, their fears and problems, and their increasing interdependence in a technologically complicated world.
The agenda at Singapore permitted wide-ranging discussions of political and economic trends in the world, of the possible consequences of the entry of Britain into the European Economic Community, of a variety of Commonwealth programs, and of the immediate future of the Commonwealth association. Canada disclosed at the meeting that it was prepared to support up to 40 per cent of the financial burden of an expanded commonwealth fund for technical co-operation. Canada also supported a less rigid format for future conferences-one which will relieve some of the unnecessary pressures now present in the preparation of an acceptable communique; one that should reduce the number of pre-prepared statements and thus permit heads of government to take advantage of the particular nature of the meetings. There was general agreement that these changes are desirable, and that the unprecedented opportunity for so many heads of government to meet regularly and informally should be jealously protected.

It is my view now, Mr. Speaker, as it was prior to Singapore, that Canada could get along without the Commonwealth but it remains my strong view that we could not get along nearly so well. No problems would be solved by the break-up of the association; not one member would find it easier to advance its own interests in its absence. The Commonwealth benefits all members and harms none. It is my firm expectation that with the help of the important Commonwealth Declaration the association will prove to be a major contributor to the enrichment of human relations. Commonwealth members share a common language. Even more important, they share a common idiom. In the result, there is permitted

an informality of encounter and a meeting of minds that surely must be the envy of other countries.
The journey to and from Singapore gave me an opportunity to travel briefly in four of the many countries which have issued invitations to visit over the past several years. Three of those countries-Pakistan, India and Ceylon-are Commonwealth members and long-time major recipients of Canadian economic assistance. Together with the journalists and photographers who accompanied me, I travelled to several of the more important of our aid projects. Through the pens and cameras of these reporters, Canadians are now more aware of the way in which Canadian funds have assisted persons less fortunate than ourselves. I found, too, that in each of those countries the earlier visits of Canadian Prime Ministers St. Laurent and Diefenbaker were well remembered. I should add that the extensive travels in 1958 of the right hon. member for Prince Albert, when he occupied this office, were brought to my attention again and again.
The fourth country visited was Indonesia, the giant of South East Asia, which Canada has recently named as a country of concentration for our aid program and one of whose outstanding citizens, General Nasution, will soon come to Canada as your guest, Mr. Speaker.
In each of those countries the program provided for discussions with the Prime Minister or President and between Canadian officials and their counterparts. These face to face encounters, and that with the Shah of Iran during an overnight stop in his country, provided an opportunity to learn at first hand of the attitudes and beliefs of world leaders in a way which cannot otherwise adequately be duplicated.
A refuelling stop at Lahr permitted me to meet a good number of our servicemen, their wives and children.

Wherever I went, Mr. Speaker, I am happy and proud to report that the name of Canada was held in warm and sincere respect. The professional dedication of Canadian representatives abroad, be they in the public service or the armed forces, serving in our diplomatic missions or in United Nations of NATO assignments, the quality of our aid programs, the value of our trade and investment relations, the friendly and positive nature of our external policies within and without the United Nations-these have all accumulated for Canada over the years an enviable reputation. I am happy to report that the resourcefulness and skills of the members of my official party and of the Canadian Armed Forces crew who were responsible for our transportation contributed not only to the effectiveness of my trip but to Canada's good name wherever we went. To them I am grateful and offer my thanks.
I have no doubt that all Canadians will agree that this high national reputation places upon our fortunate country a special obligation to conduct our affairs both internally and externally in a manner in keeping with the desire of all men to live in a world which contributes to human dignity, justice and social progress. To this end,
all Canadians must dedicate themselves consciously in order to be rid of racial or regional or linguistic prejudices for these are belittling to the world, to Canada, and to us as individuals.
In that respect, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote in conclusion three sentences from the closing remarks of Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew, Chairman of the Singapore Conference. He said:
In a multitude of ways, this conference has mirrored in miniature some of the irreconcilables the world community faces. They must be made less irreconcilable. It will become too costly and painful for mankind if these conflicts are not tempered by the spirit of common brotherhood.
Canada cannot live apart from the world. Events in far off places do affect us, as we have seen again and again in our history. If we are able to influence those events for the better, through attendance at important international conferences, and through meetings with heads of friendly states, then it is the duty of Canada to attempt to do so. This duty does not flow from some vague international role to be played by Canada. Canada must act according to how it perceives its aims and interests. It is in our interest that there not be a general racial war in Africa in the near or distant future. If the Commonwealth Conference reduced the chances of such a war, and if the Canadian delegation contributed to the success of that conference, then I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the effort was well expended.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON SINGAPORE COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to welcome the Prime Minister back to the House of Commons and to see that he is in good health after his extensive travels. He seems to have recovered well from the bout of sunburn which afflicted him in the course of his trip. I can sympathize with him in the pain of that experience because sunburn perhaps affects him in the same place as it affects me. As a result of my own familiarity with this localized discomfort I believe I shall have some insight at least into what may be one of his actions during the next week or so: when I see him scratching his head I shall know he is not necessarily perplexed-he is just peeling.
We always follow the Prime Minister's travels with interest. His most swinging encounter this trip appears to have been with an orang-outang named Joan. This adventure evidently happened during a recreational period spent in a wildlife sanctuary. Some people might accuse the Prime Minister of frivolous behaviour with Joan but I want to make it plain that I do not. I am aware of his abiding affection for wildlife and I can believe that this episode may well have been a serious discussion, perhaps about the possibility of a cabinet appointment for Joan as part of the government's current reorganization program-and I hope nobody will think I am being unfair to Joan.

speechtext: I thank the Prime Minister for his report on the Singapore conference. I share his view that it would have been tragic indeed had the Commonwealth collapsed as a result of the dispute over the British arms sale to South Africa. I understand that the Prime Minister, along with certain other participants at the conference, played a part in preventing a break-up at this time. I believe that he, as well as others who were active in this sense, deserves our congratulations.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON SINGAPORE COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
speechtext:
We must recognize, however, that the danger to the Commonwealth is not yet over. Irrespective of what happens with regard to the sale of arms to South Africa there remains a considerable amount of tension and perhaps even resentment between some Commonwealth members. I know the Prime Minister does not like the image of Canada as an honest broker, but however we may describe the role I believe this country should continue to try to retain the trust of all sides so that we can do our part to keep the Commonwealth in existence and strong.
Certainly it is a complicated institution but it has been, and remains, one of the most effective forces in the world for peace and understanding among nations. It is in Canada's interest to encourage continued harmonious relations within the Commonwealth and I hope we shall do everything in our power to this end. I am encouraged in this regard by what the Prime Minister said this afternoon.
I have already expressed my pleasure at the Prime Minister's return to parliament. In his absence the Acting Prime Minister and his other colleagues were trying, I am sure, to mind the store, but they often gave the impression of merely going through the motions. They seemed to feel that the action was taking place many thousands of miles away rather than here at home.
Unfortunately, I have to tell the Prime Minister that even in his absence Canadian problems persisted and in some cases grew worse. I presume that the Prime Minister has been brought up to date on the unemployment situation. He may remember-I am sure he will-that shortly before leaving he announced that henceforth unemployment was Canada's number one priority. I can only presume that having told the people this he forgot
Singapore Commonwealth Conference to mention it to his colleagues in the cabinet. Otherwise I find hard to explain the lack of concern they have displayed about this problem while he was away.
In fact, when the right hon. gentleman is out of the country we seem to get a more vivid and accurate picture of the kind of government that he leads. Each temporary removal of the Prime Minister's colourful wrapper enables us better to know what is really in the package. When the actions of this government are not modulated by his charming charisma in the course of their transmission to us, we get the real message, and it is an old, familiar message of arrogance and complacency that becomes less and less acceptable as times become more and more difficult.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON SINGAPORE COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the members of this party I should like to welcome the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) back from his safari abroad. In common with all Canadians, we have followed his travels with

February 1, 1971
Singapore Commonwealth Conference
great interest through television and the press and have watched him riding elephants and camels and smooching with an orang-outang.
I thank the Prime Minister for the report he has given the House this afternoon. I commend him for his statement regarding the importance of the Commonwealth and the part which it can play in the life of our day and generation. I was glad to hear him say that he thought we would gain from this association. This is a commendable change from the time when the Prime Minister, prior to a previous conference, described the Commonwealth as a useful anachronism.
3 (2.30 p.m.)
I for one do not accept the idea that the Commonwealth was in any danger. The Commonwealth is a free association of free nations working together for certain common principles and objectives. It is not necessary that they agree about everything. There is no requirement for unanimity. There can be no question of the Commonwealth trying to force its decisions or opinions on any single member of the Commonwealth.
I do not agree with the Prime Minister's statement in India that if other countries left the Commonwealth we would not want to feel less pure than they. I think it should be remembered that the men who go to these conferences to represent the various parts of the Commonwealth are simply heads of government who in a democracy at that particular time, according to the will of the electorate, head their respective governments. Governments come and governments go in a democracy but nations continue and the Commonwealth continues, and no statesman has the right to talk about taking any country out of the Commonwealth. The people are determined to stay in the Commonwealth, and I do not think any disagreement should lead to talk of the Commonwealth disintegrating.
For that reason I am all the more concerned about the whole question of the sale of arms to South Africa by Great Britain. The Prime Minister seems pleased that the amended version of the Zambian declaration of principles was accepted unanimously by all Commonwealth nations. It was accepted unanimously because it had been rendered meaningless by the Canadian amendment which said:
No country will afford to regimes which practice racial discrimination assistance which, in its own judgment, directly contributes to the pursuit or consolidation of this evil policy.
Of course, by allowing each member to decide what in its opinion is assistance to the policies of racial discrimination and apartheid it was very easy to get unanimity. I submit that the Commonwealth could have survived even had there been a difference of opinion on the Zambian declaration of principles, and that it would have been a good thing for Canada to line up with those nations who uncomprisingly and specifically condemn racialism and those who supply arms to those nations which practice racialism.

The Prime Minister said in his report today:
It is in our own interest that there not be a general racial war in Africa in the near or distant future. If the Commonwealth reduced the chances of such a war, and if the Canadian delegation contributed to the success of the conference, then I submit Mr. Speaker, that the effort was well expended.
This did not solve the problem of the sale of arms by Great Britain to South Africa; this merely shelved the problem. The setting up of the committee of eight to look into the trade routes in the South Atlantic and Indian Oceans has merit, but the whole question of whether or not we approve of the sale of arms to South Africa has been left entirely unanswered, and the declaration adopted is virtually meaningless. Therefore the problem has not been solved; it has been merely shelved. I recognize, of course, that the Canadian Prime Minister is in some difficulty in lecturing other countries about the sale of arms when Canada has been selling over $300 million worth of arms annually to the United States to carry on a bloody and senseless war in Southeast Asia. Therefore it is very difficult to lecture other countries on international morality when one's own hands are dirty.
May I say in closing that there is one thing for which the Prime Minister dan be very thankful. One of his colleagues, Mr. Milton Obote of Uganda, found that during his absence a general had taken over. I say to the Prime Minister that in his absence a general has also taken over-general discontent, with an army of between 500,000 and 750,000 unemployed. We welcome the Prime Minister back to the cold world of reality. He returns to face real problems. The Canadian people, who on television watched him playing Santa Claus round the world, hope that he will be equally generous in dealing with the problems that face Canadians.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON SINGAPORE COMMONWEALTH CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has just reported to us about his participation at the Singapore Conference. I am convinced the survival of the Commonwealth depends to a large degree on the success of such conferences. It is certainly in the interest of Canada to maintain excellent relationship with all member countries.
I remember that two years ago, I attended the Conference of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association with other hon. members. I was most interested, and mainly surprised at the vitality and vigour of the debates. Although we spoke the same language, we sometimes told each other some very hard facts but I finally understood that within an association, it is necessary to speak frankly.
I am also pleased to see that the Prime Minister during his travels has stopped in Ottawa. Frankly, all Canadians are pleased to see him back.
We are also glad that the Prime Minister has received such a warm welcome in all the countries he visited. The press, television and radio have kept us informed about those social activities. It could not be otherwise, Mr. Speaker, since Canada has been generous to those countries.
February 1, 1971

The Prime Minister of Ceylon stated that Canada was one of the most important supplier of the Colombo Plan. Indeed, the newspapers reported that before the visit of the Prime Minister to Ceylon, Canada had granted that country loans totalling some $94 million. It was therefore quite normal for that country to extend an appropriate welcome to the head of the Canadian government.
Another loan was granted to Indonesia, another country which the Prime Minister was pleased to visit.
During the past five years, all those countries received assistance from Canada which granted them interest-free loans of some $419 million, according to a reply given on June 18, 1970, to a question put on the order paper.
On his return to Canada, the Prime Minister might also decide to grant loans without interest to the provinces and municipalities of Canada, so as to allow them to undertake public works in order to relieve the misery of families affected by unemployment.
It is said sometimes that credits granted to foreign countries help them to buy products in Canada, thus providing work for Canadians. I am convinced that this is an excellent formula, and I feel that the loans that we would grant to provinces and municipalities, so as to allow them to undertake public works, would help not only to stimulate Canadian production, but also to reduce the high unemployment rate that we have presently.
I hope very sincerely that the Commonwealth conferences will be beneficial to Canada. I hope also that in the course of this year we will see very profitable results ensuing for Canada from the last conference.

In view of the request of a number of the provinces for the early establishment in Canada of a guaranteed annual income, and in view of the support for such a program by all parties represented in parliament, this House now declares its support, in principle, of a guaranteed annual income for all Canadians, and urges the government to introduce such a plan at an early date.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Skeena has filed a notice as required under the terms of Standing Order 26 and which has given me the opportunity to give serious consideration to his request. The subject of his proposed motion, as outlined by him, is similar to others which have been made from time to time upon the publication of statistics relating to unemployment. The last requests for such motions were made by the hon. member for Spadina and by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands on January 14 last. The reasons outlined in the ruling denying those motions, as reported at page 2397 of Hansard of January 14, 1971, would appear to apply in the present circumstances.
As hon. members know, we have just recently had a two-day debate on the subject of unemployment. That took place on January 18 and 19, the House dividing on an amendment by the hon. member for Edmonton West. That was on the third and fourth days of the budget debate. As hon. members also know, Standing Order 26 provides that the Speaker should take into account the probability of the matter being brought before the House within a reasonable time by other means. There are still two days available to hon. members for completion of the budget debate. Indeed, the Standing Orders will provide a number of other opportunities for further discussion of the unemployment situation.
In view of the provisions of Standing Order 26 and in light of all the circumstances, I must conclude that the hon. member's motion should not be put to the House today.

The House resumed, from Friday, January 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Drury (for the Prime Minister) that Bill C-207, respecting the organization of the government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto, be read the second time and referred to the committee of the whole.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is very important that we have a thorough debate on Bill C-207 in view of the wide range of subject matters involving government operations that are covered by this bill. I recognize the unavoidable absence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) recently, but at the same time I think it important that he be present during this debate, and that we hear from him about some of the implications and consequences that flow from the changes that are proposed in Bill C-207.
I did note that when the Prime Minister returned to Canada from the Commonwealth conference he chose to make a reference to the business that has been dealt with by the House of Commons during his absence and indicated some impatience with the progress being made by the House of Commons. Just what the reason is for this impatience I find difficult to tell. As a result of this comment, I took the time to review the matters dealt with by the House of Commons during the 15 days since we recommenced the session on January 11.
First of all, we have spent four days on this bill, the government reorganization bill. I suggest it was necessary to spend this time in view of the many matters the government has chosen to include in the bill and in view of some of the consequences of it. Two days were spent on the budget debate. I would ask whether the Prime Minister feels we should not have spent those two days on the budget, since they were devoted by agreement to a consideration of the very serious unemployment problem facing Canada. We spent two days on the young offenders bill, as a result of which the opposition persuaded the government to delay further consideration of the bill until it had considered some representations that have been made and reviewed its position. I suggest that, in taking this stand on the bill, the opposition was fulfilling one of its responsibilities in this House. That disposes of eight of the 15 days.
[Mr. Comeau.l
I do not want to deal in detail with the remaining seven days, but I do wish to point out to the Prime Minister that the House of Commons gave third reading to seven items of government business. Most of those bills were of some importance and consequence to Canada as a nation. One bill received second reading and then went through the report stage. There was also a motion to refer a subject matter to a committee of the House of Commons. I suggest that, in light of the business dealt with during the absence of the Prime Minister, the House of Commons has in fact been carefully discharging its responsibilities during that period.
To turn to Bill C-207 now before the House, I may say I took note of the comments made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), who introduced this bill on behalf of the Prime Minister on January 26. At the conclusion of his speech, he asked for the co-operation of hon. members in giving the bill careful consideration and speedy passage. I suggest that there is a conflict between those last two phrases, "careful consideration" and "speedy passage", for the reasons I have already enumerated.
The fact is that in this bill we have a mish-mash of many aspects of government operations. Possibly there is some justification for including some of them in the same bill, particularly those items dealing with executive functions and executive operations of the government. However, also included in the bill are some very important provisions that involve new precedents and departures from principle as they relate to the public service of Canada. Just what sort of rationale the government used in putting together these two areas, matters dealing with the executive functions of government and matters dealing with the public service, I fail to see.
I think there are implications in the decision the government made to include all these items in the one bill. In fact, I think this points to the view of government that is held by those on the treasury benches. As pointed out by some other members, we really have a group of technocrats running the government. I think this point was made very well by the President of the Treasury Board who, in introducing the bill on second reading, said as reported on page 2769 of Hansard:
In essence, the government organization bill deals with the constant challenge facing Parliament and the government-
Then, the first point he made was this:
-to be as efficient as possible in doing those things which are in the interest of the Canadian people and society.
I suggest that this is the view of a technocrat. To be fair, I should also point out that the minister went on to mention the changes taking place in Canadian society, and said there were implications for the relationships between governmental institutions and our changing society. Nevertheless, the first point he made was the one of efficiency. It is the view of some technocrats that an attempt should be made to make efficiency an end in itself rather than a means to an end.
I suggest that the government needs to give more consideration than it apparently has to some of the implications that flow from the bill now before the
February 1, 1971

House. One of the most important of these that I feel requires consideration is the balance between the executive arm of government and the legislative arm of government. In recent years we have witnessed an increasing concentration of power in the hands of the executive branch of government. We have had any number of examples within the past two or three years which indicate that the sole concern of the government has been to increase the power of the executive branch.
One example, of course, was the introduction of the roster system, and the manner in which the government did it. I want to say that I sympathize with the situation of ministers generally, in view of the very wide range of responsibilities they face and the difficulties imposed on any group of human beings in discharging these responsibilities. Again, I would have to point out that what we had was the imposition of this roster system on Parliament with some unfortunate consequences. I should have thought it would have been quite possible, by following a procedure of negotiation and the exercise of a little patience, to have worked out a system that would have been acceptable, to all concerned. In fact, I suggest that, in the long run, the government would have been caused less trouble than it has had as a consequence of the manner in which it imposed this new ad hoc system.
We had the introduction of regional desks in the Prime Minister's office. Again, this involved a concentration of power and a bypassing of Parliament through the setting up of independent machinery which was responsible only to the Prime Minister. I think this has resulted in an imbalance of power in our governmental structure.
Then, as well, we had rule changes, some of which were introduced by the government. Most of these rule changes, I think, met with the general approval of members of the House of Commons. However, I suggest that the intent of the government in forcing through some of these proposals, and in particular Rule 16a, was to disrupt the proper balance between the executive and the legislative functions of government.
There are also consequences arising out of the use of the committee system and some of the changes which have been made in the operations of the committees of the House. I do have to say in that context that I think all of us recognize that, to some extent, we are experimenting. We are in an experimental stage in dealing with the rules which relate to the operation of the committee system as it is presently embodied in the structure of the House of Commons. There are some satisfactory aspects to the operation of committees, but I think there are also problems that have to be taken into account. I think the fact is that the committee system, as it has operated over the past two years, has in effect reduced the power of the House of Commons in areas which are the proper jurisdiction of the House of Commons.
Another area in which there have been developments relates to the increase in staff and the increase in powers and functions of the Prime Minister's office as well as the office of the Privy Council. This aspect is well known to
Government Organization Act, 1970 hon. members and again can only result in a further imbalance of power. As a matter of fact, there are some suggestions that this change has resulted in some imbalance of power within the Cabinet itself. The suggestion is that the result has been to concentrate power in the hands of the Prime Minister and those around him. The developing trend, therefore, has been a rising growth in ministerial staffs. This is, of course, related to the increasing role that Parliament or government must play in our society. This, by itself, should not be criticized. It simply must be noted when we are taking into account the changes which are to be made in the executive and legislative functions of the government.
We have a further growth in the ministry. This, of course, has to do with the executive branch. There is provision for a number of ministers of state within the government. We are going to have more Parliamentary Secretaries and a larger cabinet. Possibly they are needed and possibly further development is needed. I am not going to argue against these changes in view of the very important role the government must play in our society today, but again we have the government concentrating the growth in the executive function and the power of the executive. I think the question must be asked, where is the balance in this situation? I think the power of Parliament to act has been reduced, and this has been noted by many parliamentary authorities on the constitution and government of Canada. Comments to that effect appear in a number of texts which I could cite if necessary. These authorities have, in fact, pointed out that, in many respects, Parliament is in the hands of the Cabinet. I suggest that the power of Parliament has been reduced, in particular in dealing with money matters. This, of course, goes to the very core of the Power of Parliament as we know it, and as it must function if we are to preserve and develop our parliamentary institution.
There have been a number of token gestures to help the opposition parties in particular, and private members in the House of Commons, including such things as extended research assistance. Of course, this assistance has helped the private member and Parliament, but I suggest that in no way does it begin to offset the increasing power of the executive as we have seen it. While I am on this subject, Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to note, as I have had occasion to do during some other debates in this Chamber, the comparisons that are often made between Canada and Great Britain. I believe the President of the Treasury Board made similar references when he was introducing this bill.
The fact is that while our parliamentary institution and our system of government has been modelled on the British parliamentary system, we do have to keep in mind the fact that Canada is a different sort of country. In the first place, we have a federal system of government rather than a unitary system. This imposes some very fundamental differences on the way in which government operates. We are at a different stage of development. The geo-economic structure is different, and I think as such it imposes some real differences on the operation of government and our parliamentary institution.

February 1, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
While at this stage I should also deal with some of the provisions of Bill C-207 concerning the ministries and ministers of state. I know that some rather extensive powers are to be given to the Governor in Council in deciding on the need for a new ministry of state. Clause 14 of the bill, if I might be allowed to quote briefly from it, reads:
Where it appears to the Governor in Council that the requirements for formulating and developing new and comprehensive policies in relation to any matter or matters coming within the responsibility of the Government of Canada warrant the establishment for the time being of a special portion of the public service of Canada presided over by a Minister charged with responsibility for the formulation and development of such policies, the Governor in Council may, by proclamation, establish a Ministry of State for that purpose.
True enough, this does introduce some flexibility into government operations. It also begs some questions and it leaves some questions hanging in mid-air. For one thing, it seems to me in reading over this particular clause, along with some of the others, the question of the status of these ministers of state within the government and the Cabinet is left in the air. It seems to me there are some unexplained aspects and areas which are not completely clear. Will these ministers be of Cabinet rank or are they in fact going to play some different sort of role within the government?
In addition, I also note that there is no time limit in respect of the phrase "for the time being". It seems to me that the use of this phrase does suggest this is a temporary arrangement or an arrangement which is of limited duration. However, since there is no provision to limit the existence of these new ministers of state, we could see a new ministry of state established, as is provided for in clause 14, for the time being, which in fact became a permanent institution. It would then have been established not by this Parliament but by the Governor in Council. I suggest this is not the proper way to proceed with the business of government. I also note that power is given under clause 15 to transfer functions from other departments or other agencies of government to one of these new ministries of state.
I suggest that here is another important consideration. If parliament does vote money for the use of an agency or a department of government and then the reorganization is carried out, under the provisions of this bill power is given to transfer some of that money from existing agencies or departments to this new ministry of state, and this new ministry of state may in fact be constructed on an entirely different set of principles. In fact, the establishment of this new ministry of state may involve completely new departures from government policy. The departures from government policy may be completely acceptable to Parliament, to myself and to other Members of Parliament, but the fact is that the government is given the power in this bill to transfer moneys which have been voted for one existing structure, and presumably a certain set of policies which go along with it, to a new agency which may be operating on a completely different basis. Of course, that would apply only within
the fiscal year in which the particular change occurred, but again I suggest it is a violation of the principles of parliamentary government and of the control of Parliament over money matters.
I think also we must keep in mind what is happening with regard to the collective ministry. Here, I note one of the comments by the President of the Treasury Board. He suggested that the warp and woof of our ministerial system is very complex. I am not quite sure what interpretation might be placed on that remark. The interpretation of some people is that things are going to the dogs. Certainly, there is a good deal of foundation for that belief. I think the government is warping many of the responsibilities which they have been called upon to bear, and with respect to the woof, there are indications that many aspects of our affairs are going to the dogs.
We have to keep in mind what is happening to the various ministries because it would appear that the government is embarking on some new departures in policy with regard to the ministry. It would appear that the government is perhaps taking a partial step at least towards the British system which does involve a separation of the functions of the cabinet and of many of the ministries which exist within the British government. I suggest that we need a clearer elaboration on this particular point, and on some of the implications and consequences of the provisions of this bill with regard to the over-all operation of government. I suggest, with all due respect to the President of the Treasury Board, that this can only come from the Prime Minister. This is why we need to hear from the Prime Minister in this debate. I want to make clear that I feel there will be many occasions in dealing with the problems of society as they exist today when it will be necessary to have special agencies such as are provided for in the sections dealing with the establishment of various ministries of state.
However, I think we do need to reconsider some aspects of this particular portion of the bill. At the same time, I should also state that reference has been made to the possibility of appointing a minister of state for science policy. We are going to have a minister of state for urban affairs and possibly in some other areas of government activity as well.
There is one particular area to which the Prime Minister should give his attention. I refer to the very serious state of affairs that exist in Canada today because of the fact that the rural society in Canada is disintegrating at present, in some cases as a result of policies and in others because of the absence of policies. At present we have a number of departments of government which are concerned with one or more elements of rural affairs in Canada, but nowhere do we have a co-ordination of those efforts. The Department of Agriculture, of course, is involved; the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has also been involved in rural problems and rural affairs. A number of other departments must of necessity be involved as well, each with their own particular area of responsibility. But nowhere do we have a co-ordinator, at least in terms the public can identify or that can be identified by members of the House. Thus, I would sug-

February 1, 1971

gest that in a reorganization of the government consideration should be given to the establishment of a ministry of state for rural affairs. I will not attempt to spell out any thoughts I might have at this time concerning what it should include or how it might be structured. However, I feel there is a good case for giving consideration to the establishment of such a ministry which could co-ordinate the activities of the government in dealing with the problems of rural Canada which are very serious indeed and which, I feel, must be taken into account by the government in the near future if we are going to salvage any sort of viable rural society in Canada.
One of the more important aspects of the bill has to do with the establishment of a department of environment. 1 noted very carefully the remarks of the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) who is the minister designate for this new department. I noted also some of the steps that are proposed and some of the steps which are being taken to deal with the problems of pollution and environmental planning. I am sure all hon. members will agree with those steps. I think that this is a very important new department of government. I suggest that when we are dealing with problems of pollution and of environmental affairs and planning, in fact we are dealing with some of the crunch issues that face society today, both in Canada and in other countries. The fact is that the state of our environment, its deterioration, is one of the causal factors of the social discontent in our society today. I say that because in today's society young people in particular note that there are two particular elements present around them which could result in an end to human life on this planet within their own lifetime. One is the threat of nuclear war, and the other is the possibility of environmental deterioration which would make life on this planet no longer possible. I suggest the realization that there are elements present about us today that could result in a termination of life does result in some of the impatience which we see about us in society and some of the discontent which we have seen expressed in so many forms within recent years.
In dealing with the new department, I think it must be noted that this is where we will have a crunch between government and industry. This is where we are going to face the crucial issue of whether industry will be required to operate in the public interest or whether it will continue to be allowed to operate strictly for its own profit, its own narrow interests and benefits. This is where we are going to face some crucial issues, such as whether or not the government has the determination to ensure that industry in fact takes the necessary actions to develop a better environment so that we all might live healthy lives.
There are two or three other issues which I should like to mention as well in dealing with the new department of environment. One has to do with the potential conflict which I feel must be taken into account and which should be drawn to the attention of the House. The department of the environment will be concerned with all aspects of the natural state of life, and this will have particular consequences in northern Canada where the ecology is very fragile. On the other hand, the Depart-
Government Organization Act, 1970
ment of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources are more concerned with the economic and commercial development of that area. It seems to me that there is ground for potential conflict within the framework of the departmental structures as proposed in this bill, taking into account this area. It is a problem which must be noted by hon. members, and by the government in particular.
I find it difficult to understand why the government dos not propose to transfer the national parks service to the proposed department of the environment. It seems to me it is a natural for inclusion within that department. This is an agency dedicated to the preservation of certain areas in their natural state for the use and benefit of all our people. But it is not being transferred to the new department. It is being left with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, even though responsibility for the Canadian wildlife service and for the Migratory Birds Convention Act is being transferred to the new department.
The bill proposes the establishment of a Post Office Department separate from the Department of Communications. This, of course, involves a rather long, sad story which I do not intend to relate at this point. However, I would like to take this opportunity to place one matter on record again, the matter of rural postal service. I am very much concerned about it because I have had to deal with a number of problems in my constituency, and I know the problems in other areas of Canada, where the withdrawal of postal service seriously affected rural communities. I must say that in some instances I could not argue against the withdrawal of postmasters from small communities, but I wish to place on record once again a proposal which I made when I was speaking in the Throne Speech debate last October. I see no reason why we could not develop a sub-post office system in some rural areas similar to that which operates in large urban centres. I see no reason why we could not have a main post office located at some central point, with a number of sub-post offices operating under its jurisdiction to ensure an adequate standard of postal service for all the settled rural areas of Canada.
Much has been said during this debate about the proposed amendments to the Public Service Superannuation Act. Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, I take serious objection to some of the provisions in this respect. I fully sympathize with an attempt on the part of government to introduce a greater element of flexibility in its personnel management policies. Certainly, I am not going to stand in the way of any reasonable steps which will enable the government to deal with its personnel-management problems in a better way, but I am not prepared to support a measure which will provide a degree of favouritism to some people in the public service which is not available to others. I feel that these proposals in Bill C-207 are very objectionable.
This is one of the most important pieces of legislation to be brought forward during the current session of

February 1, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970 Parliament. I am very unhappy at the government's handling of the bill, and at the manner in which it was introduced. I am very unhappy when I think of some of its implications and consequences, and that is the reason for my intervention in the debate today.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first remarks in connection with this bill on the fifth day of debate are to express a rejection of any question of an apology for a continuation of the debate. I can only express regret that the Canadian media have seen so little in this bill which is about to transform the structure of parliament, of the Governor in Council, and the relationship between the two. They have been deluded, as in the past, by siren songs of efficiency, of flexibility, and themes of that kind. And yet every time that this is done it is done at the expense of parliament, at the expense of the House of Commons.
This is another slice of the salami sausage, only this time it is a big chunk that is being taken. I shall go into that in greater detail when I discuss the proposals to set up the ministries of state and then, by proclamation, make the necessary changes. It seems that this administration has forgotten one fundamental principle. This House is not responsible to the cabinet, nor does it owe obedience to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The Governor in Council is responsible to this House, but to see it behave, to see what the Governor in Council wants to do, you would never believe that. It rides roughshod over the principle of having to come to this House to justify its actions.
Every time we give the Governor in Council power to do something it is an abdication; it is a laissez-passer; it is a carte blanche to go and do something without telling parliament. I know it will be said, "well, there will be provision in the estimates thereafter." Just whom are they trying to fool? Is the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) going to try to substantiate that argument, that there is control by authorization after the event, that there is control after the payment of the salary of a minister? What debate is there on the salary of a minister? What debate is there now on any estimates? What opportunity is there for justifying the restructuring of government? Mr. Speaker, government is responsible to this House. This House is not a tool of the cabinet. But this cabinet is composed of technocrats and former bureaucrats who insist that this House must be molded, must be trapped, must be formed into some complacent organization. It makes me think that in the minds of those who have designed this they wish a rubber stamp assembly, merely to say yea or nay, much as we see in various countries around the world operating under despots, benevolent or otherwise.
In precisely a bill of this kind, and by this devilish principle, you can see the manacles being fashioned to be tied to hand, to wrist, and to ankle of this House. Oh, it will be made to sound very plausible, very smart, and acceptable under the guise of so-called efficiency and flexibility. The government backbenchers have been

hoodwinked all the way through. Some additional parliamentary secretaryships have been thrown to them as a sop. They are just pennies for children, candies for grasping, greedy kids.

That is what this is. There is no need for all these new parliamentary secretaryships. We shall see, when we see the final composition of the ministry with the four categories of ministers, just how big the cabinet will be. I suppose that a parliamentary secretaryship will become a first rate status symbol. Parliamentary secretaryships will become status symbol No. 1. The government will appoint a few more members from the backbenches who have had no experience of parliamentary secretaryship. May I say that I spent many years as one. I have some idea of the duties of that office, of the potential of that office and how few ministers are able to recognize the best way to use their Parliamentary Secretaries to full advantage. Most ministers have been scared of their Parliamentary Secretaries. They are frightened they might take some of the shine away. This has been one of the facts of life in the past. That appointment was made as a reward on a regional basis, or for good attendance, or far too often for some other capricious reason. On the other hand, there have been some very notable exceptions of ministers who understood how to use a Parliamentary Secretary. Such ministers used the Parliamentary Secretary to his best advantage and, as well, for the general benefit of the department and of the minister. I will deal with that question in a moment.
Having said that, I hope, for goodness sake, that the press, the radio and television, instead of chasing their tails like puppy dogs on other fluffy issues, will look at this particular bill and see how serious it is. Oh, there has been mention of it, but that has been in passing. The hare is running another way and they all want to chase after it. Yet the principal game is here, in the consideration of Bill C-207, and they ought to pay attention to this debate.
I want to join in the general resentment and objection to the omnibus nature of this bill. I made some remarks to Your Honour at the opening of this stage of the debate about that matter. I have noted Your Honour's remarks and, of course, do not question your decision. Yet I wish, with the greatest of respect, to underline to the Chair the absolute requirement, and I say this in all seriousness because I have had some experience in that position, that any question put before the House must be capable of resolution in a clear and straightforward manner, readily understood by hon. members. There must be no tricky solutions. Yet, Mr. Speaker, this bill, to import a phrase, is too clever by half. It is a contradiction of principles. Oh, we were fed some pap the other day.
We were told that this bill was for the greater efficiency of government. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) said that the underlying principle of the bill was the more efficient organization of the government. What a lot of nonsense that is. As I said to Your
February 1, 1971

Honour, we could take all bills relating to one ministry and lump them together into an omnibus bill. I suppose then that we should consider 15 or 18 bills during the year. For instance, we could take all the bills dealing with trade and lump them together. My assertion that the urgency of this matter has been increased is based on two propositions. The first of these propositions is an obvious one, one which, no doubt, hon. members had in mind when I said there was urgency, namely, the increase in the cost of living and the difficulty that many of our senior citizens are having in living on the amount of income that they now receive. Despite the provisions that were made in a bill which has already been passed in this session, and which we must therefore not refer to in the course of this debate, the amounts that will be available in April still do not bring our senior citizens up to the poverty line. That is one of the points of urgency that I feel make it imperative that the government and Parliament reconsider the whole question of the provisions of the Old Age Security Act.
I said, however, that there were two bases for my using the word "urgency", and in my view the other one is even more serious, if not quite so precise as the dollars and cents angle I have just been speaking about. The other element of urgency arises from the fact that the government in its white paper on income security has come out clearly and definitely for a lessening of the application of universality and for greater use of selectivity in all of our pension, welfare and security programs. I know that the government does its best to marshall arguments. I know that it quotes figures, that it tries to tell us that universality is out of date. But I suggest that this declaration by the government that it is going to move in the direction of selectivity rather than

February 1, 1971
Old Age Security Act
universality is a case of going the wrong way and that it will yet destroy our whole social security setup.
I know that there is a great deal of talk about what we are going to do for the poor, whether they are senior citizens or the working poor or any group in our society. But I do hope that some day we will get to the realization that it is not good enough just to do things for the poor and keep them that way. When we do things for the poor because they are poor, they are poor at the end of the road. This is not good enough for a society that is capable of producing the amount of wealth that we can now produce in this country. If we are going to do something for people and not hurt their pride and dignity, not do damage to their souls in the process, we should do it for them because they are people and have rights as people. In my view, the day will come when even our attitude toward jobs and toward being employed will change. Now, you are not a first class citizen unless you can get a job, and if the job is non-existent, you have to fall back on some form of unemployment insurance. When it is gone, you have to fall back on social assistance, relief, welfare, or what have you.
I firmly believe the day will come when all people in a democratic and decent society will be guaranteed the income to enable them to live as a matter of right, whether or not they get attached to an existing or a non-existing job. I want us to move in that direction, and back in the early 1950s I was glad when we started to move in that direction by putting our old age pensions on a universal basis. Like other members in this House, I have had enough experience with older people to know that that legislation did a great deal for the sense of pride of our older people.
Now that we are going in the other direction, we are losing much of the gain that we made by that course of action. Therefore, I suppose this is a case of starting all over again. It took us many years to get the means test removed and to put the old age pension on a universal basis. It stayed that way for a decade and a half. Now, because the government has announced it is going the other way, some of us have to start all over again. If that is the case, I suppose that is what I am doing today. By this motion, I am saying we are starting all over again to try to win the battle for old age pensions to be paid to all our people as a matter of right. Let us not talk about any war on poverty, about being concerned about the poor, or about the dignity of our people if we are going to require these means and incomes tests. If we really mean what we say about dignity and the rights of our people, let us determine that our legislation will provide a proper standard of living, first of all for our older people, then for our families, and for our citizens generally, not because they are hard up but because they are people.
I need not make the point that I do not stand alone in my contention that universality is a much better principle to work on than selectivity, but I would like to read a few sentences on this subject which I thought put the point very well. They were contained in a brief that was drawn up by the Canadian Council on Social Development in December, 1970. These are comments on the position set out in the white paper so far as the govern-

ment's old age pension position is concerned. At the point in this document from which I shall read, reference is made to certain dangers and then the following statement is made:
A major example ol this inherent danger is the unfortunate polarization of the argument about "universality versus selectivity" in the white paper on income security.
I have said that I am a universalist, but I am happy to subscribe to what I now read in this paragraph. It goes on to say:
The two are not necessarily incompatible, granted effective use of the income tax system. Progressive income tax is the fairest way we know of raising money for social purposes. If it is wisely employed in relation to income security measures, the desirable features of selectivity can be achieved while maintaining the most important advantages of universality. Indeed, it is noteworthy that the white paper on unemployment insurance argues strongly for the principle of universality (which the white paper on income security appears to denigrate) in support of its proposal to include all members of the labour force in the program, whether or not they are likely to benefit by it.
I might say that in this same document the Canadian Council on Social Development-which we knew for so many years as the Canadian Welfare Council-complains about the level of benefits under the Old Age Security Act not being high enough and also about the fact that those on the basic pension will not get the cost of living escalation. But I come back to the portion of a sentence in this paragraph which I have just read which it seems to me is very significant, "If it is wisely employed"-that is, the income tax principle-"in relation to income security measures, the desirable features of selectivity can be achieved while maintaining the most important advantages of universality." If I understand that right, and I think I do, it says very simply that it is far better to make a universal grant, whether it is the old age pension or what have you, and tax those who, because of that grant, get into higher income brackets, than it is to test people's income before you give them something that should be their's as a matter of right.
I say again, Mr. Speaker, that I think the Liberals of the early 1950's, and they were in power most of that decade, were right when they agreed to our demand to take the means test off the old age pension. I think that the Old Age Security Act which was passed in 1951, and came into effect on January 1, 1952, was the best and most progressive piece of social legislation ever passed in this House of Commons, and I am proud to have had a part in seeing that this was done.
Far from accepting the statement that some of us are old fogies because we want to stay with that principle that was brought into effect in January, 1952, I suggest that that is the way to achieve a just and decent society, not to call upon people to disclose their means before they get something that is handed to them because they are poor, but to grant pensions, allowances, and soon, I hope, a guaranteed annual income to all our people as a matter of right.
This is private members' hour, Mr. Speaker. I have now taken up 13 or 14 minutes of it. I know what will
February 1, 1971

happen to this motion. Debate will still be taking place until you, at six o'clock, tell us you are leaving the Chair until eight o'clock. So, I do not expect it to come to a vote this afternoon. I do not expect to win this battle this month, perhaps in the next little while, but I do ask hon. members of the House to give serious consideration to this whole question. I will listen to argument. Others have their right to present their points, as I have mine, but I submit we are going in the wrong direction by taking away universality from the old age security pension. I urge that we get back to that principle as soon as we can and, when we do it, that we establish the pension at more realistic levels, such as $150 a month with the right of everyone who is on the pension to the cost of living escalation.
I will not take time to answer the arguments that I know will be made about the cost and all the rest of it. We have been over that ground many times. We can afford in this country what we want to do. If we want a decent, just society, if we want people to have their share of the affluence we are able to produce, we can order our affairs accordingly. This motion asks that we take this one important step in that direction, and I hope hon. members will give it favourable consideration both in this hour and in the thinking about old age pensions that they will do, as they must, in the months that lie ahead.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gaston Isabelle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT TO INCREASE PENSION AND GRANT COST OF LIVING SUPPLEMENT WITHOUT MEANS TEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I repeat that it is always an honour for me to have an opportunity to deliver a speech during the private members' hour, particularly on as significant a subject as that dealt with in the motion put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I am satisfied that he has long been concerned with the welfare of elderly Canadians. I hope he will pursue this laudable objective, especially with regard to subjects involving persons of a certain age who served well the Canadian community.
The hon. member must also be commended for stating that the Liberals of the early '50s were progressive and enlightened men because they passed legislation on this most important question of old age security pension.
I must say that even though they were right in 1950, they did not think perhaps that one day they would have to take new measures and adjust to other circumstances. Many changes have occurred since 1950 and many more will occur in the future. In 1950 these people were wrong about income security especially with respect to people who retired at 70.
I should say also that at that time oil heating was far less popular than it is today. In fact, many people still burned coal for heat. If we had not evolved and since today coal is increasingly rare, I wonder where we would be.
In fact, changes are happening so' fast that one must keep up with the times. The present government, like those that preceded it, has to go through some sort of readjustment made necessary by present circumstances.
Old Age Security Act
I also know that the hon. member is in favour of a universal plan as opposed to a selective one. This is all very natural since his party is essentially socialist. In fact, the New Democrats shun like the plague anything that is selective by nature. They insist on giving a little to everybody and, the end result is that nobody gets anything.
In any case, this philosophy is far remote from that of the present government and I take this opportunity of expressing my appreciation for it because given our present circumstances and more specifically the amount of public funds at the government's disposal, it is unthinkable that with the financial resources available we should give out more money in all directions as we would like to do.
Unfortunately, with the responsibility to govern comes also the responsibility to redistribute the money at our disposal.
As far as the arguments of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre are concerned I recognize in part their value. He and his colleagues are trying to get into power. I do not say that they are using the right means to do it but it seems to me that they used one of those means. Indeed people who are not in power say a lot of things which generally may sound pretty good to the press and to the public. But when one takes a serious look at the issue one realizes quickly that it is inconceivable to satisfy everybody by passing uniform acts in order to make every body happy.
When you have lived for a while you know that it is impossible to please everybody. It is inconceivable that everyone should be happy in this valley of tears of ours. Even tremendous amounts of money cannot satisfy the rapacity, if I may call it so, of human nature.
Those who have something want a bit more, and those who have more want even more than they have, and so on, until death.
But I should also like to mention that the federal government-

speechtext:
I was alluding to the liberals, Mr. Speaker .. . I should also like to mention that the liberal government-how strange that the word should always find its way to our lips, that even our adversaries should be forced to use it-belongs to the elite of Canadian society.
The federal government has been legislating in the field of social security since 1927. It started by granting a modest pension of $20 per month to which the provinces contributed. In 1931, the federal government decided to contribute 75 per cent and in 1949, the amount of the pension was raised to $40.
But on Friday, I heard one hon. member say he was surprised at the speeches full of substance that had been prepared in dusty offices of some officials. I think that to make sensible and rational speeches, one must be rather well informed and from what we hear in this

February 1, 1971
Old Age Security Act
House, it is not easy. I do not know whether this is due to excessive smoking, but it seems that there are hazy periods in some poor brains, at least judging from what they say.
In spite of the hon. member's comments, I would like as much as possible to stick to the text which I had the pleasure to draw up with some officials, because as I said a while ago it is difficult to memorize all relevant statistical data. Moreover, it is the custom in the House when a question is put to government members to consider statistics to be out of order. This is normal.
Indeed, the public life of Our Lord lasted three years. I do not know whether he studied from early childhood until age 30, but at 33 years of age, he died under the tragic circumstances with which we are well acquainted. This is why it is unthinkable that I could give you specific information gathered for quite a long time. Indeed, somewhat like Our Lord, I came into political life a little late and I did not have the astuteness of some members who have spent almost all their life behind those oak walls where stiffness and coldness usually prevail.
I would like to keep to a text, as much as possible, because it contains some extremely interesting figures.

Since its introduction, the Old Age Security Act has been amended on a number of occasions. The rate of benefit was increased twice in 1957, first to $46 monthly and then to $55. In 1962, it became $65, and in 1963 the monthly pension again was raised, when it reached $75 a month. It remained at $75 until 1968 when, because of an amendment enacted in 1965, the pension could be escalated each year depending on, and in accordance with, changes in the pension index used for the Canada Pension Plan. Provision was also made in 1965 to reduce the pensionable age under the old age security pension program one year each year so that the OAS pension would be payable in 1970 to all persons aged 65 and over. As a result, the percentage of elderly persons aged 65 and over covered by the OAS program increased from 66 per cent in 1965 to 91.8 per cent in 1969 and very close to 100 per cent in 1970.

I must say that this is an extremely important thing, since it deals largely with the problem of money expended for this program.
I would like to say also that-

By 1970, the Old Age Security pension was $79.58 monthly and the maximum guaranteed income supplement amounted to $31.83, for a combined total of $111.41 a month, but by the end of that year the OAS pension scheme had been amended again following the proposals set out in the White Paper on Income Security.
Under these new changes to the Old Age Security Act, which received Royal Assent on December 18 as we know, substantial improvements have been made to
benefits payable under this income support program for our senior citizens and improvements have been made with respect to its other features. The basic old age security pension has been set at $80 a month while the maximum supplement, payable to elderly persons with little income other than the old age security pension, has been raised to $55 monthly for a single pensioner and to $95 a month for a married pensioner couple. The 1971 maximum supplement will increase by 72 per cent for single pensioners and by about 50 per cent for pensioner couples over what it was in 1970.
In 1960-61, and this is very interesting, Mr. Speaker, the expenditures under the Old Age Security Act were $592.4 million and represented 1.55 per cent of the Gross National Product. Between that year and 1969-70, the value of the Gross National Product more than doubled, but costs in the same period under the OAS pension legislation, which by then included the guaranteed income supplement program, nearly trebled to $1,730 million, so that in 1969-70 OAS/GIS benefits to aged people represented 2.16 per cent of a much larger GNP. These costs are therefore growing at a faster rate than Gross National Product, which means that a greater proportion of the nation's resources are being channelled into this program for the aged. These amounts exclude any payments or assistance received by elderly persons under any other programs, whether government or privately administered, which, if included, would increase the proportion of GNP just mentioned.
The hon. member has recommended that each elderly person now eligible for the old age security pension should be paid a basic $150 a month, escalated each year by the full increase in the cost of living. Let us consider the financial implications of his proposal. Taking the fiscal year 1969-70 as an example, old age security pensions and guaranteed income supplements payable in this year totalled $1,730 million. If instead all OAS pensioners received $150 a month, total expenditures in that year would have been $2,809 million. His proposal would involve an additional $1.1 billion. Based on estimates for fiscal year 1971-72, annual expenditures under the new OAS/GIS amendments legislated for in 1970 and which will come into effect on April 1971 will total $2,183 million, whereas under the scheme proposed in this motion expenditures would amount to $3,108 million. From these data, it can be quickly calculated that paying all pensioners $150 a month would cost the country nearly $900 million more than the recently amended Old Age Security Act.
Further, if these dates are projected and if the base-year benefits are escalated at 2 per cent a year, costs in the fiscal year 1975-76 under the amended Old Age Security Act are estimated to be $2,450 million, while those under the proposal suggested in this motion would amount to $3,680 million, more than $1.2 billion in extra expenditures. This means that in four years the additional cost of the proposed scheme under motion 13 will increase from $900 million to $1.2 billion over the new OAS/GIS program. Not only are these additional costs

February 1, 1971

large, but they are becoming larger and larger as time goes on. Surely the hon. member is not suggesting that the taxpayers of this country can afford this additional load in one particular sector of the income security system. As it is, the latest amendments to the act will place an additional $200 million into the hands of the most needy elderly persons in the current year. Hon. members will agree that is a substantial sum of money.

Any good government will try of course to provide as much social security to the taxpayers as possible but as I said at the beginning the financial means at the disposal of the government are limited. However through his white paper the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) is trying to ensure better distribution of the funds at his disposal.
To me, the principle of redistribution is the most important today, much more so than in 1950.
The same thing probably applies to family allowances. It is obvious that if our resources are distributed exclusively to one population group, as proposed in the motion, we will necessary have to neglect the other Canadians. Even those who are unemployed will be deprived of certain financial resources if we put all our eggs in one basket.

Another factor is that the hon. member is suggesting a return to the type of program based on an approach of universality, while the philosophy of the white paper on income security suggests selectivity in income security. Universality was important at one stage of the development, but social and economic change indicates that a selective approach is a much better technique. This change is explained in the recently issued white paper on income security, part of which I quote as follows:
The challenge, then, is to arrive at a renewed affirmation of income security policy which will have the effect of assisting the people in the greatest need without detracting from programs designed to stimulate the economic development which is the basis of national well-being.
