Order. I regret to interrupt the Parliamentary Secretary, but his time has expired.
Mr. Jack Marshall (Humber-St. George's-St. Barbel:
Mr. Speaker, I will speak for only a few moments. I support the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), with one reservation. My main concern is for the aged in this country who are suffering from exceptional incapacity. The white paper on income security states that after April 1 old age pensioners will receive $135 a month. This is certainly below the poverty line. Hon. members forget that there are old people who cannot look after themselves. There are people in my province who are crippled because they worked for many years trying to make a meagre living. They live alone in hovels. They need a tenants' allowance in order to acquire proper accommodation. When they ask for increased benefits, we cannot supply them.
Old Age Security Act
The previous speaker referred to the great cost in providing additional benefits. The state owes the aged of this country a decent living, a living at least above the poverty line. The motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre does not ask for too much; it asks for $150 a month. As I stated, I have one reservation. I do not agree that a man of 65 years of age earning $25,000, $30,000 or $35,000 a year requires such a pension. I do not agree with a universal, across the board pension of $150 a month. I say, with respect to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that if he inserted an amendment which would require a means test I would support the motion to increase the old age security to $150 a month. That would be little enough, Mr. Speaker. The government should forget about bandying around figures and talking about the millions of dollars it would cost. There should be no end to this bucket. I say that old people who are exceptionally incapacitated should receive more.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT TO INCREASE PENSION AND GRANT COST OF LIVING SUPPLEMENT WITHOUT MEANS TEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is to be congratulated on bringing this motion before the House. As everyone knows, he is an outspoken advocate on the problem of old age pensions. We are happy to have an opportunity to debate this motion this afternoon. The hon. member spoke on television last evening in a similar way. He will be pleased to know that at least one of the members on the government side took time to listen to his dissertation. The hon. member proposes that old age security benefits be increased to $150 per month for everyone 65 years of age and over. If this were done, we would be able to do away with the guaranteed income supplement which we passed only a few weeks ago.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has suggested that the urgency for bringing forward this motion is the increase in the cost of living. He has also argued the question of universality versus selectivity. I suppose that is the real argument. To be against this motion would be to be against motherhood. We are really debating whether $150 per month should be available across the board regardless of the income of the person receiving it or whether it should be available on the basis of a means test.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). He is a very capable member of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. He handles himself well in that committee. He opts for the selectivity approach rather than universality. I have forgotten all the figures mentioned by the Parliamentary Secretary as to the increased cost of a universal as opposed to a selective program. However, one figure that sticks in my mind is that there would be an increased cost of $900 million over the present program. As the number of our senior citizens increases, this amount will increase.
One aspect which has been brought to my attention by people concerned with welfare in my constituency is that people receiving old age security benefits and the guaran-
2956

February 1, 1971
Old Age Security Act
teed income supplement are not eligible for general welfare assistance, except perhaps for drugs. It seems to me that when the federal government is negotiating the terms of the Canada assistance program with the provinces, some provision should be made to meet the needs of people in exceptional circumstances, people receiving old age pensions, to qualify them for special assistance should the cost of housing, for instance, be unduly high or should some other special need arise.
Income maintenance for this group of the Canadian population has been the subject of numerous revisions and adjustments from time to time. Income maintenance payments for aged persons made under federal programs amounted to $773 million in 1962-63. The figure had risen to about $1,950 million in 1970-71, just short of a threefold increase. Older Canadians now receive income protection through a number of measures both public and private. Under public programs income support is available under the Old Age Security Act, the guaranteed income supplement, retirement and aged survivors pensions under the Canada and Quebec pension plans, and supplementary social assistance under provincial welfare programs, the costs of which are shared by the federal government under the Canada assistance plan. In the private sector, income protection is provided through private pension plans or various self-help measures such as annuities and other privately-arranged retirement schemes. Public and private programs which provide income support are important to elderly people. It is also important to ensure that a wide range of health, welfare, recreation and other services are provided to meet the needs of this group.
I should like to review the needs of elderly persons for benefits in kind or services. Canada's first century of progress was characterized by the pioneering of young people. Only in comparatively recent years have we become fully aware of the special circumstances of the aged in our population. Changes in this aspect of our development have come upon us faster than we have been able to prepare for them. There are greater numbers of older people than ever before, and the number continues to rise. The urbanization of our society, employment practices, inflation and rising costs of living have all contributed to the changed conditions for older persons. Since families live in smaller homes and in apartments, there is less room to accommodate aged members of families. There are fewer tasks for old people to do in the home, and too often they are left out.
I turn, now, to population and life expectancy in Canada. The 1.6 million persons aged 65 and over in Canada represent slightly less than 8 per cent of the total population. Thus, while Canada may be regarded as having a low percentage of older people when compared with some other countries, we are experiencing serious and increasingly complex problems for which there are no simple solutions. Life expectancy at birth for both males and females has risen substantially over the years. On the other hand, although the number of aged persons has increased, only small gains in life expectancy can be reported for those who reach age 65. But while improvements in life expectancy are important, of equal or perhaps greater importance is that the quality of life be improved. The problems of the young have become of such concern that they have to a major extent absorbed the creative energies as well as the economic resources of communities. All too often, therefore, there is little left to invest in improving the quality of life of the older sector of the population.
Hospital care is available to all residents through provincial hospital plans by means of a cost-sharing arrangement with the federal government. The majority of the provinces are participating in medical care plans in which the federal government shares in the costs. For the indigent, payments for health care are assured by the provincial governments, with costs shared by the government of Canada under the Canada Assistance Plan. This plan is designed to provide increased federal aid, thereby enabling the provinces to integrate, expand and improve their welfare assistance and service programs.
Aside from health care there are some services specified in the legislation which can be of special assistance to the aged. I refer to case work, counselling, assessment, information and referral, home-maker or home-help and day care. In some places hot meals are delivered to older persons at midday in their own homes. Arrangements to live with private families, the so-called foster care programs, are being developed in some areas. Nursing care for the aged in their own homes is also provided in many communities. Senior citizens centres have been provided in some places, where the aged can go for recreation and in many cases receive a range of other services. Hundreds of clubs have been organized, some of them by older persons themselves and others by churches or other agencies. A national organization of older adults has been established with branches in most of the provinces. It is interesting to note that nearly all these groups presented briefs and wrote to many Members of Parliament during the past year and a half while we were reviewing the old age security program and the guaranteed income supplement.
The Canadian Council of Social Development, which was formerly called the Canadian Welfare Council, has concerned itself over the years with matters pertaining to the aged and aging. Some provincial and local welfare councils have established sections on the aged. Service clubs have been actively engaged in organizing and helping older persons in many localities; for example, they have developed senior citizen centres in housing projects. These service clubs as well as churches, fraternal organizations and other voluntary agencies frequently engage in providing recreational programs for the aged. Grant programs organized by the Department of National Health and Welfare, as well as grants from federal funds allocated to fitness and amateur sport, have provided funds for research and demonstration programs which directly or indirectly will improve the care of elderly persons.
I should now like to refer to the provision for living accommodation for aged persons. In all provinces, homes for the aged and infirm, including nursing homes, are provided under provincial, municipal or voluntary aus-

February 1, 1971

pices. The provinces contribute to the maintenance of needy persons in these institutions, 50 per cent of the payments in respect of assistance cases being met by the federal government. All provinces, in varying degrees, make capital grants toward the construction of homes for the aged and infirm and in some provinces capital grants are also available to municipalities, charitable organizations and non-profit corporations for the construction of low-rental housing. According ot the 1961 census, of the
747.000	heads of households aged 65 and over, almost one-quarter lived alone. It is within this group of older adults-those who live independently in their own homes, whether owned or rented, and whether separate dwellings, flats or apartments, as well as an additional
198.000	elderly persons who live with relatives-that the need for community services exists.
An attempt has been made to describe in a very general way the programs available to serve older persons in Canada. But the gaps are many, and too often even existing services fall short of being able to meet the needs. It is generally agreed that older persons should remain in their own homes in the community for as long as possible. To achieve this goal, a range of community services designed to provide the necessary care of the appropriate type and of the quality and quantity required is essential. Moreover, these services have to be readily available to persons in both urban and rural settings.
In Canada the emphasis has been upon institutional care. This is due to many reasons, including distances to be travelled, difficulty of staffing programs in more isolated areas, limited professional resources and inappropriate living arrangements for aged persons. Thus, when communities have turned their attention to the needs of the aged they have tended to plan first and, all too often, for the construction of institutional care facilities only.
An added complication arises when an old person is in hospital and is ready for discharge to a lesser level of care. Frequently there is not a bed available to provide the care he needs in a home for the aged or a nursing home. Even if there is, he may resist transfer because payment is made on his behalf under the provincial hospital plan for as long as he is in a general, chronic or convalescent hospital, whereas for institutional care, or care in his own home, with few exceptions he must pay for services himself in so far as his financial resources permit. In order to encourage older persons to remain out of institutional care, it may be that we shall have to consider paying for community services so that institutional care offers no financial advantage. For any special services which may be needed by only a limited number of persons, payment may have to be based upon ability to pay.
It is roughly estimated that from 5 to 10 per cent of aged persons require some form of institutional care. Some 20 to 30 per cent are in need of intensive supportive services within the community at large. The remaining 60 per cent are well, ambulant individuals functioning independently in the community. We see them every
Old Age Security Act
day going about their affairs; we do not think of them as aged. Indeed, if we are suddenly asked to focus our attention upon the needs of the aged, those living in institutions first come to mind. We think of the bedridden, the frail and the sick.
More emphasis should be placed on keeping those aged persons who are well and actively carrying on their affairs in that happy state. Preventive health measures, such as disease detection screening programs and early treatment of conditions found through such programs, should be intensified. Since it has long been recognized that chronological age is a very unsatisfactory determinant in deciding the ability of a person to continue in employment, there should be greater flexibility in respect to the age of retirement. It is, however, a proven fact that fewer persons at age 65 wish to continue in employment than was the case 25 or 30 years ago. Technological advances are beginning about even lower ages for retirement in some industries. Further, by actual choice, increasing numbers of persons are voluntarily choosing to retire earlier than age 65.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT TO INCREASE PENSION AND GRANT COST OF LIVING SUPPLEMENT WITHOUT MEANS TEST
speechtext:
As soon as I finish my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I shall be glad to give the hon. member an opportunity to pose a question. Without becoming involved in the pros and cons of arbitrary versus more flexible retirement arrangements, there is no doubt that society still equates productivity with monetary reward; that is, life earning a living. There is a consequent loss of status for the majority of persons at retirement. But some older persons have perceived "productivity" in terms of service to their community, in service to contemporaries and in creative achievements. The aged represent a vast resource of human abilities and skills which society has been overlooking.
Some older adults are asking: What can we do to help ourselves, each other and the community? Many are simply continuing to serve within the community as they have all their lives, but others are offering themselves for the first time, sometimes for service on a voluntary basis, sometimes for pay. Older adults are very strongly motivated to engage in various programs through a desire to help others. Even those who are not in the best of health report that having something to do for others keeps them active.
In summing up, may I say that aging, a lifelong process of growth, development and change, begins before birth and progresses at different rates and in different ways in every individual, depending upon genetics and environment. Just as each phase of a person's life cycle is determined by those which have gone before-adulthood, adolescence and childhood-so also is the preparation for a successful and satisfying life in later years a lifelong preparation. A first requirement is good health care, including the application of all known aspects of preventive and restorative health practices, so that we do in fact attain complete physical and social well-being to the greatest degree possible. Further, every individual needs

February 1, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970 to develop interests, retain and sharpen his curiosity about the world around him and participate in lifelong education whether formal or informal.
There is no single problem of the aged. Rather, there is a whole complex of problems-health, housing, jobs, family and community relationships, attitudes and so on. Planning in terms of older persons requires a realistic approach to the problems on a wide variety of fronts. We need to apply new knowledge, new concepts and new techniques as these emerge. We must learn to live with change and to direct it. We must continually remind ourselves that effective solutions are intimately related to the conditions under which we live, and when some of the conditions change we must adjust other aspects of our lives to these changes. We need to be experimental, creative and imaginative in developing programs to meet the challenge of the later years and in accord with the society in which we live.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Drury (for the Prime Minister) that Bill C-207, respecting the organization of the government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto, be read the second time and referred to the committee of the whole.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been discussing these past few days Bill C-207, entitled an Act respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto.
This bill provides for the reorganization of several departments and the establishment of the Department of the Environment. The minister in charge of this department will assume all the responsibilities of the Department of Fisheries and Forestry while receiving new
powers in order to control the pollution of the environment.
As regards this scheme, I remain rather sceptical. It appears that this is an improvement over present efforts to solve the problem of water pollution and it is obvious that immediate steps must be taken in that respect. But I am wondering if those that are proposed in the bill will be adequate and effective. As a matter of fact it is not because there is a Department of Agriculture that all farm problems have been solved. Neither did the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce put an end to all bankruptcies across the country.
I hope the public will not be under the impression that the proposed department is the answer to all problems relating to pollution, because in any event it is a very serious one.
Let us refer to an article in La Presse of Wednesday, June 11, 1969, under the by-line of J.-Claude Paquet, entitled: Water pollution is beyond control, and I quote:
"Water pollution is overtaking us at a frightful speed. One may even affirm without a doubt that it is beyond control." This statement was made yesterday by Dr. Richard Nelson of Hull, a member of the water development committee of the Quebec Wildlife Federation.
Assembled at Manoir Richelieu for their annual convention, the engineers and technicians of the water development association expressed their concern-
Speaking in a somewhat reproachful tone, Dr. Nelson told members: "You fully realize that you have retreated too long behind the imperviousness of your discipline, only allowing scraps of information to leak through, uninclined to launch a sustained campaign against water pollution.
Deficiencies responsible for the present situation are to be found at all levels of our community.
A large measure of the blame should be placed on the silence of the experts on water in the face of what is happening.
According to the lecturer, organizations dealing with Quebec's water problems have given the impression, up to now, that all is for the best in the best of possible worlds and that the higher authorities have the situation well in hand.
Mr. Speaker, we can imagine to a certain point all the publicity which will accompany the setting up of a department of the environment. We know that new regulations will be issued if they are required. Actually, some very logical ones have already been in existence but they were practically never implemented. I would like to quote a report which was published in the newspaper Action on September 22, 1969:
Our natural environment has a tendency to depreciate slowly! "The fast depreciating and often non-reversing condition of the natural environments needed for recreation is a by-product of our industrial society". This serious accusation against our modern way of living was brought by Professor Robert Lagueux, during a lecture that he delivered at the conference on water problems during the weekend in Quebec.
According to him, this degradation has been taking place at such a pace, especially for the last ten years or so, that one can truly speak of a clogging of the natural cycles of recuperation and self-purification of the environment.
This problem is so serious that it endangers the survival of man, Mr. Lagueux told us. In his opinion these ever increasing dangers result from the arrival on the market of these multiple-use chemical products with unknown side effects.
According to the lecturer, we are embarked in a vicious circle.

February 1, 1971

We waited until the situation became urgent before taking steps and securing the services of television, newspapers and radio to do some advertising.
I remember quite vividly the recommendations made by the federal government a few years ago with regard to farmers. I recall among other things that they had been instructed never to dump insecticide containers into rivers or lakes.
During the same period, with the federal government's blessing, the Canadian Corporation for the World Exhibition dumped thousands of gallons of DDT around the Expo grounds. Since these were islands in the river, the St. Lawrence was completely polluted, so much so that today we wonder just how much longer the fish will survive.
Nowadays, publicity is made at the housewife's expense. She is told what detergents to choose while she only uses a few gallons of water a week to do her washing.
I would therefore appreciate it if the sponsor of this bill could tell us whether the government has asked the pulp and paper companies, which pour their residues 24 hours a day into the river, to change acids.
Pollution of the soil, pollution of the sea, pollution of the air, pollution of the water: there is pollution everywhere. Let us wage war against pollution as we are doing against poverty.
The number of unemployed and of those who have tighten their belts in the face of affluence is a concrete proof that there is also, within the government, pollution of the mind, pollution of the intellect.
One thing is sure: that the government is about to increase taxes. On January 26, 1971 La Presse reported the following statement made by a bank manager. I quote:

"Canadians must be willing to forgo affluence so as to palliate the cost of pollution, said last night the Chairman of the Bank of Montreal, Mr. G. Arnold Hart. However, the public must be cautioned-"
-about what is forthcoming.
"Because the problem is really there: any effort against pollution will result in economic restraints, added the banker who explained however that "it is much too easy to demand that the cost of pollution control be paid by those responsible for pollution".
"All of us create some pollution and we must all pay the cost, either by accepting an increase in prices or in taxes, or by forgoing certain goods which seem very desirable, or by putting up with the unemployment caused by the closing of industries incapable of complying with new standards."
This is a bank manager who says that: factories will close down, the number of unemployed will increase, taxes will be increased. So as to satisfy the voracious appetite of the banks, the people will have to tighten their belts. Privations and reductions, that is good enough for the people. Meanwhile, banks bring up their interest rates. It is possible that this expert, a bank manager, will go as far as getting his salary increased.
And who knows if the increase in the assets of the Bank of Montreal, which was 33 per cent for 1969-70,
Government Organization Act, 1970 will not reach 50 per cent. Anything can happen since this bank is one of those which can tighten or loosen credit at will.
We remember quite well the years 1929 to 1939 when credit was under strict control. It had been enough that the word "war" be used for all the banks to grant more credit. We are still paying for this supposed favour. The people have lost from it and so have the provinces. We remember that under the pretense of temporary measures which were to last during war time only, the provinces had agreed to part with some of their taxing powers. To save Christianity and freedom the provinces had yielded. Unfortunately, more taxes are levied so that people enjoy less and less freedom and communism is spreading throughout the world.
Taxes were increased to establish the family allowance plan. These taxes have gone up but family allowances have remained unchanged. Other taxes were imposed to cover the increase in old age pension. Other collection methods have been created under the pretense of fighting poverty. The number of poor people is increasing but we still have the same methods.
The government, which has been fighting inflation by new taxes and restrictions, is now launching war against pollution because our major businessmen have finally agreed to co-operate.
We have known capital shortages but surely our businessmen will put an end to them to fight pollution.
In return, the citizens' work will still be taxed, and so will building materials, clothing and many other life related commodities.
In setting up this new department, I am convinced the government will find a way to tax the air we breathe.
Clause 5 of the bill reads as follows:
5. The duties, powers and functions of the Minister of the Environment extend to and include all matters over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction, not by law assigned to any other department, branch or agency of the Government of Canada, relating to
(a)	sea coast and inland fisheries;
(b)	renewable resources, including
(i)	the forest resources of Canada,
(ii)	migratory birds, and
(iii)	other non-domestic flora and fauna;
(c)	water;
(e) the protection and enhancement of the quality of the
natural environment, including water, air and soil quality;
With regard to the soil, Mr. Speaker, we must get acquainted as soon as possible with all available research in this field.
As to air, which changes in colour from one region to another, action should be taken as soon as possible.
In the case of water, studies involving the various aspects of water resources management have been carried out in the province of Quebec and elsewhere in Canada. These studies lead us to confirm that from a legal as well as practical standpoint water supply and treatment fall mainly under provincial jurisdiction.
However, in view of the inter-relationship of water related problems in the different areas of the country, we must recognize that the provincial framework is hardly

February 1, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
adequate if we want to approach their various aspects efficiently. Some of them are of Canada-wide concern.
We do not necessarily conclude that it is either mandatory or desirable for the federal government to assume full responsibility over the water question, but that it should rather take a keen interest in all aspects of the various Canadian problems.
The water question can be broken down into three parts. First, municipal and industrial water supplies.
In this regard, it is generally recognized that to date provincial jurisdictions have fulfilled their tasks adequately. Drinking water is available in adequate quantity and quality as well in Quebec as in the rest of the country.

Then there is the comparatively new problem of sewage treatment whose solution is to be found mainly in a collective desire to take the appropriate measures. Purification costs remain almost the same whether the undertaking is achieved under the federal, provincial or municipal government or with industrial participation. In this connection, the federal government can and must help financially to make up for inequalities and take the necessary measures.
Finally, as water is a basic element in our environment, the part it plays should conform to the ways of life followed by all Canadians. In this respect, the approaches may differ from one province to the other; however, a general notion of the minimum requirements is essential and the federal government can and must assume a constructive role in determining the goals.
Under every aspect of water management, each level of government should discharge its responsibilities within the framework of our Canadian political institutions and in a spirit of co-ordination and co-operation. Any federal government initiative or arrangement likely to impede the action of a provincial jurisdiction would act contrary to the results looked for.
On the one hand, the federal government's action must be very strong in the fields where it has exclusive powers, but on the other hand it should be complementary only in the fieds that traditionally come under provincial jurisdiction.
Nevertheless, in their own interest, the provinces should take advantage of any financial or technical aid available from the federal government. In our opinion, initiative and planning should remain in the hands of the provinces. Besides, the federal government can and must act as a catalyzer of public opinion, guiding the choice of national goals and choosing measures calculated to create a collective will aimed at correcting the situation.
To that end, we suggest that the complementary action of the federal government deal with the following aspects: research, technical information and popular education. There must be co-ordination in research and information. All Canadian citizens must be sensitized in a rational way to the problem of water and environment.
Minimum criteria should be established on the quality of water and wast° in co-operation with the provinces. A
step has already been made in proposing Canadian standards. There only remains to complete them.
The government should, in co-operation with the provinces, make an inventory of the water resources of Canada. Although each province is interested in that inventory, the general picture must also be considered.
It would be necessary to set up mechanisms of federal financial participation based on long term estimates of financial needs. In other words, we suggest that spending estimates be made for each province as well as for the whole of Canada. The allocation of expenses, for each level of governments and for all the users, must be made according to these estimates within the framework of an orderly financial program.
Every effort must be made to find more equitable and more rational financing methods. In the immediate future, municipalities and industries are confronted with a financing problem which impedes the implementation of the required programs. The federal government can give essential financial aid and must give it without delay.
In the issue of October 3, 1969 of La Presse, one could read a statement by the then Minister of Resources, who said:
-that some Canadian firms will be forced to close their doors because of the government antipollution program.
During an interview, the minister explained that pollution was at the present time everybody's problem, but that the pollution caused previously by certain firms was their direct responsibility.
Some industries might not be able to pay for measures to fight pollution and will then have to shut down.
Mr. Speaker, if industries are forced to shut down, due to lack of funds, I think there is a serious problem and before spending millions here and there to start new industries we should find ways to save those that already
exist.
The same thing goes as far as public undertakings are concerned. Public needs may be urgent, well detected, expressed and understood by public bodies, but if those bodies have no money or not enough, the implementation of plans is delayed.
What is missing, then? There is no lack of materials. We know that manpower is abundant. There are plenty of competent people. Finally, the only thing missing is money, financial credit.
In short, with or without this new department, the pollution problem in our country is becoming a financial problem. There is no going back. The co-operation of the public, the provinces and municipalities is necessary, but the essential steps cannot be delayed. However, we know that in the present system, most public bodies are deep in debt and can no longer consider any development, even in the case of pollution which is a matter of life or death.
It is obvious that it is only by incurring other debts at a 10 per cent interest, that we could reimburse our old ones and carry out the necessary pollution control programs.
As the government is the supreme authority in this country, I wish it would prove its capability by demand-

February 1, 1971

ing that the Bank of Canada grant to the provinces and municipalities which might request them interest-free loans similar to those granted foreign countries.
I agree that we must set up programs to control soil, air and water pollution, but if we really want to do it we should first wage war against financial pollution by reorganizing the Bank of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, on rising to comment on Bill C-207 I wish to associate myself with those hon. members who have already expressed objection to it. I do not believe it is necessary to go into detail on the aspects of an omnibus type bill other than to state that all too often in this Parliament we have seen a few goodies thrown in with a bag of tricks in one piece of legislation, parts of which are unpalatable but which are presented to Parliament for approval.
This bill gives the government power to expand, to spend and to entrench without recourse to the representatives of the people. From now on a ministry may be established simply by proclamation, something which is completely contrary to the traditions and precedents of our parliamentary system. This bill reaffirms the trend of the present administration toward the establishment of a bureaucratic dictatorship. It also reaffirms the truth of the often used cliche that the Liberals are concerned with expectations of power-patronage in perpetuity.
When we look at the potential expansion of ministries combined with the expansionary provision for parliamentary secretaries, we can see that this bill, if passed, will give everybody on the Liberal side a chance to be somebody; and the suggestion is that they had better behave and support the government or they will find themselves among the minority group classified as nobodies. I suggest this would be extremely disastrous for them when they face the electorate in the next election, and that applies even to my hon. friend from St. Boniface, Manitoba.
With the exception of that portion of the bill which proposes the establishment of a department of the environment, of which I approve although I suggest it is a rather feeble and cursory attempt to strike at the "gut" issue of pollution, I see nothing in the bill which will give any measure of ease to the many Canadians suffering economic burdens and miseries. The creation of a department of the environment will be in fact a nonevent. I submit that the bill should establish a comprehensive administrative structure to fight pollution. Instead, it proposes a piecemeal structure which will have incomplete power. I say this because the acts to be administered by the new department were drafted for other diverse purposes and will not provide the new minister with sufficient regulatory power to undertake a comprehensive campaign against pollution. Indeed, if the government is serious about a comprehensive and planned attack on pollution, it must introduce comprehensive regulatory powers directly intended for this department to enable it to carry out its ambitious responsibilities.
Government Organization Act, 1970
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, the bill offers nothing in the way of a measure of ease to alleviate the burdens, miseries and pressures which affect so many Canadians today. On the contrary, they will be asked to dig deeper into their pockets to finance the rewards to be handed out to Liberal members who have distinguished themselves as well-disciplined, well-behaved boys fully endorsing the policies and trends of their seniors. I am given to understand that already the impact of the bill has been felt in this regard. I am told that many Liberal members who wanted to speak on the bill have been asked to refrain from participating in the debate. This is the brand of participatory democracy in which the government believes, the kind in which Liberals cannot afford to disagree.
To the more than three-quarters of a million Canadians who are presently on unemployment insurance, to the many, many more living in poverty without access to public assistance, to the old age pension recipient, to the war veteran, to the many small businessmen who have been forced to close their enterprises and to the many, many more on the verge of closing because of the government's perpetrated economic crisis, to the many, many small farmers and to some not so small who have been attempting to eke out a living on 63 cents per bushel for barley and $1 per bushel for wheat, of which 50 per cent is retained in respect of previous advances, this bill offers no hope and is nothing more than a clouding of the issues.
This bill deserves nothing more than contempt, because the government simply does not care. It cares not about those who are unable to assert their rights and privileges because of lack of organization or political power. The people in these groups are suffering the gravest injustices in our society. This government with callous and coldblooded disregard simply carries on building its empire and its bureaucracy. It is creating positions which will do nothing but increase frustrations and complicate the channels of redress for those attempting to obtain consideration for their plight.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that until the war on inflation was won there was little hope of relief for those struggling at or below the poverty line. The Prime Minister now states that inflation is licked. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that those were nothing more than empty words. I remind the Prime Minister that only because of lower food prices the cost of living index levelled off and reduced. Speaking as one who represents an agricultural area and many agricultural producers, I hope the Prime Minister does not expect producers and retailers to bear the brunt of the war on inflation. I hope he does not expect us to fight inflation single-handledly. I submit that if the major food chains declare a truce, we shall again experience a rise in the cost of living.

Mr. Speaker, some aspects of Bill C-207-are of vital interest to my constituents. I refer to the creation of a department of the environment. I believe this is an important step forward. If the department is given the means and the tools to do the job, it may play an important role in the meeting the environmental crisis.
I do not wish to detract the very reasonable criticisms of my colleagues about the hodge-podge of different subject matters brought under the cover of this bilL That is extremely unfortunate. However, I do not propose to deal with that aspect of the matter. I shall deal with the subject of pollution of the environment particularly as it affects areas such as the one I represent, the metropolitan area of Toronto. It is trite to say that we have reached the situation in which the unintended result of our practices has been to threaten animal and plant life and to destroy the environment on which the quality of human life depends. There has been no lack of warning. In the course of this debate, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) drew attention to a declaration of the United Nations in 1968 which gave that warning very clearly and explicitly. I will not repeat what he said.
We should pay close attention to that warning. It refers to a crisis of worldwide proportions. It refers to the explosive growth of human population, poor integration of a powerful and efficient technology with environmental requirements, the deterioration of agricultural land, the uplanned extension of urban areas, the decrease of available space and the growing danger of extinction of many forms of animal and plant life.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), when he was Acting Prime Minister a short time ago filed a report on pollution of Lake Erie and Lake Ontario. It was an extensive and full report of the International Joint Commission. Lake Ontario and Lake Erie are two of the greatest freshwater lakes in the world. While the report refers to one part of the country, similar problems have arisen in nearly all the great waterways and freshwater lakes in Canada. I quote from the conclusions reached by that commission as follows:
In response to the question, "Are the waters of Lake Erie, Lake Ontario, and the international section of the St. Lawrence River being polluted on either side of the boundary to an extent which is causing or is likely to cause injury to health or property on the other side of the boundary?"

The commission finds that the waters referred to in the question are being seriously polluted on both sides of the boundary to the detriment of both countries and to an extent which is causing injury to health and property on the other side of the boundary.
In response to the question, "If the foregoing question is answered in the affirmative, to what extent, by what causes, and in what localities is such pollution taking place?"
The commission finds the polluted waters are lakewide in extent; that the two principal causes are wastes discharged by municipalities and industries into the above waters and their tributaries; and that pollution is taking place in all jurisdictions whch share these boundary waters.
The report goes into greater detail in the lull text. The third question was as follows:
If the commission should find that pollution of the character just referred to is taking place, what remedial measures would, in its judgment, be most practicable from the economic, sanitary and other points of view and what would be the probable cost thereof?
The response was the following:
The commission finds that the remedial measures include the adoption and adherence to this commission's general and specific objectives as a matter of urgency; immediate reduction of the phosphorous content in detergents; the prompt implementation of a vigorous programme to provide the necessary municipal and industrial waste treatment facilities and to reduce the phosphorous inputs into the above waters and their tributaries-
And so on. Later in the report is a series of detailed recommendations spelling out what ought to be done- the setting of water quality objectives for these boundary waters, as they are called, among other things. The tragic part of all this is that a report in almost exactly similar terms-and I have it here-was made by the International Joint Commission as long ago as 1952, I believe it was, and very little or nothing has been done about it. The International Joint Commission exists by virtue of a solemn treaty made in 1910 between the United States and Britain, representing Canada at that stage of history, in which both countries pledged themselves not to pollute the waters in the other country. Yet this pollution has been going on since 1910 and was reported on fully in 1952 without, as I say, anything being done about it.
This is why I am glad to see specific reference to the matter in the bill before us. Under clause 5(g) the proposed minister of the environment is to be given jurisdiction in connection with the enforcement of any rules or regulations made by the International Joint Commission in respect of boundary waters, as far as pollution control is concerned. This task alone is a tremendous one for the new department and I earnestly hope it will be carried out.
I wish to call attention to two points with regard to the whole question of pollution of the environment. First, on the question of enforcement: there have been many studies made and much research done in the pollution field, and there is need for more studies and more research; but all the studies and research in the world will not enable us to deal with this question adequately unless there is adequate enforcement. I hope the minister will

succeed in getting an effective staff on the enforcement side. I hope he will get people who are not only trained in the law but who have the required energy, tact and determination to enforce the legislation in co-operation with other jurisdictions.
The other thing that is required is consultation with informed and interested local organizations. I am happy to see that many of these are springing up. In this connection, as well as in connection with the point I have just made about the necessity of adequate enforcement measures to ensure that the rules made are not disregarded, I refer the minister to a new body known as The Canadian Environmental Law Research Foundation. I do not know whether the minister is aware of this association. It is a group of mostly younger lawyers in Toronto; I am sure they will soon spread out on a national basis. I wish to read what they say about their purposes, because this is of great importance. They say the following:
In downtown Toronto people choke and wheeze. Elsewhere In Ontario fishermen and Indians lose their source of livelihood when the fish become contaminated with mercury. Vacationers turn away as mounds of green algae pile up on the beach. What can they do about it?
Growing numbers of Canadians are seriously concerned about the deterioration of their environments. Groups have sprung up across the country which, each in their own way, attempt to meet the pollution crisis head-on. Whatever they do to arouse the public, however, they are ultimately faced with the realities of the Canadian political and legal system.
If we are to proceed in an orderly fashion to solve some of these problems quickly and rationally, current law must be put to better use and new approaches must be explored. Given the constitutional and jurisdictional complexities of resource management in Canada, an all-out effort must be made by the legal community to assist in the formulation and, more important, the interpretation of legislation for the management and control of the environment.
Recognizing, however, that in a democratic society the public must understand and be able to utilize the law, we believe that citizens must be educated as to the legal recourse offered them. Unfortunately, the Canadian public and, indeed, most lawyers remain largely unaware of the existence of such remedies.
Recently a group of lawyers and law students, brought together by a common concern for their imperilled environment, formed the Canadian Environmental Law Research Foundation. Although a separate entity, it will work closely with Pollution Probe.
I urge the minister to get in touch with this organization and consult them in the development of his staff. Unless he has on his staff people who are not only knowledgeable about such matters as prosecutions but are endowed with the requisite tact and judgment to enable them to co-operate with other law enforcement jurisdictions, I fear the department of the environment will not carry out the purpose to which it is dedicated.
I wish to speak, now, about another organization which exists in my own constituency and which has concerned itself deeply with the question of local pollution, something which closely concerns federal jurisdiction and the proposed new department. This organization is called ForWARD 9, "ward 9" being the municipal designation of part of the area covered by the riding of Greenwood. It is a non-partisan, voluntary citizens' organization. It has formed a pollution task force which has surveyed the nature of the source of pollution in the area. Its findings draw attention to what are probably the three main

polluters: the Richard L. Hearn generating station of Ontario Hydro which is, itself, a creature of the Ontario provincial government; the municipal incinerator on Commissioner Street operated by the metro works department, part of the municipal government; and the main sewage treatment plant on Ashbridge's Bay, also operated by the metro works department. It turns out that the three main polluters are all public organizations, so the report throws light on what is likely to be one of the main problems in this field.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I echo the sentiments of most members of the House who have spoken so far. I echo their expressions of concern for the environment and their good wishes to the minister. I think these expressions were sincerely put forward. If not totally sincere, they were at least put forward out of a very deep and continuing sense of concern for the condition of our environment and our seeming inability to cope with the problem as time goes by. I join these people in wishing the minister good luck in the task that faces him. No minister in Canadian history has faced such a monumental job with such a total absence of sources of information, guidance and precedents. As well, no minister, at least in my opinion, faces the task that is ahead of him with better skills, talents and, I am sure, more sincerity and dedication to the task of bringing some rhyme and reason to this headlong rush of madness that we are facing.
If I may be permitted one other comment in connection with the minister's very real responsibility, it is this. I hope the minister will have the fullest support not only of the cabinet in its present configuration but as well in its proposed configuration. I am a believer in numbers and I believe there is strength in assistance. Whether or not the minister will get that support every time he asks for it in trying to clean up all aspects of our environment and all the problems of pollution remains to be seen, but I have some confidence in his ability to get it.
Like my colleagues who have spoken before me, I express concern over the downgrading of our fisheries. 1 trust that in practice this will not take place. I am prompted to raise this question because of the very startling step taken today in closing down the swordfishing industry. The implications of such a move are very serious. I hope the minister is much more on top of the situation than the news that has come to our attention so far would indicate. The closure of this industry means the loss of a swordfishing fleet of 40 to 60 ships, involving 300 to 400 men and their families, not to mention the supporting services of the industry and the satisfying of the palates of thousands of North Americans who enjoy swordfish as a delicacy.
The source of mercury pollution in fish must be identified rapidly, not only to save the industry but to preclude the fear and panic that I think the minister is well aware could spread among those who enjoy this food. I am terrified that one morning I shall wake up and find the pollution situation so bad that I have to give up eating mackerel, lobster, tuna, cod, hake and halibut. The minister shakes his head, and I pray to God he is right-that this is just an isolated incident, a phenomenon of the industry. However, it is still my understanding that the source of this pollution has not been identified. The causes are not completely understood, but I hope they

With regard to the minister's department, like everybody else I have been waiting very patiently for a long time, realizing that the minister has no clear precedent to guide him-

The minister says they cannot pay for it without the legislation. If the President of the Treasury Board would get on his feet and guarantee that the new minister of the environment will be given the necessary funds to clean up the Great Lakes, the oceans and our northland, I am sure the co-operation of the members on this side of the House would be very readily achieved. To come back to the question of money, so far no member on the other side of the House has dared even to approach the question of the cost of cleaning up our environment. Yet this must be done. The people of Canada who so anxiously await the steps to be taken by the minister also await a price tag. So I repeat the words of the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau): it takes money to fight pollution, and money must be forthcoming if we are to survive and not permit raw sewage to be dumped into our inlets, harbours and bodies of fresh water. I was going to mention the Ottawa River, but that is a moving body of water. Perhaps I should confine my remarks to bodies of water that do not have self-flushing capabilities.
One of the first steps the minister should take is toward stopping what is taking place. He should not accept suggestions and proposals which would only perpetuate in one way or another the problem we are attempting to attack. If we are to clean up pollution, let us at least start by putting an end to situations which permit new pollution to creep into our environment When new plants are built, let us insist upon standards which are high enough to be effective and keep the air clean. Let us apply the same principle and influence in respect of the effluent that pours into our rivers, lakes and oceans. Let us put an end to this pollution quickly.

In spite of the difficulties the minister will face in the coming months with the type of legislation and regulations required, he will find comforting support among his colleagues in the House of Commons. I hope he is aware of the fact as he steps forward armed with his new legislation.
One might argue that it is a form of pollution to allow governments and societies to continue to discard policies before they have been effectively used, policies which have been demonstrated to be effective but which are changed in some way to meet the demand for change. This happens frequently. It seems to me that those who are filling responsible positions have been by and large useless. The cabinet system has not been a bad one up to now. The worst I can say about it is that I think it is in the wrong hands. Our system of government seems to have worked fairly well for a number of years but I am not at all sure it has not outlived its usefulness. That is one of the conclusions one must draw from what appears to be the intent of this legislation. It seems to discard other policies simply because change seems to be the desirable thing. When we discard ideas and concepts before they have fully served the needs of society, we have wastage-and that is pollution. As my leader said some days ago, this is prideful pollution and it is unnecessary at this time. It is wasteful in itself when it has not been demonstrated to the satisfaction of the people of Canada that there is a real need to expand the cabinet.
The people of this country, through their representatives in the House of Commons, are being asked to accept this open-ended legislation. This is wrong, if the legislation is placed in the hands of those who would use it for other than correct purposes, in terms of our understanding of the political system. Sometimes I wonder just what is the concern of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government in proceeding to this extent. What does this all mean, and how far do they intend to go? What is their intention? Apart from the department of the environment, for which there is an obvious need, why do we need these open-ended ministries of state? They are very loose in their application.

I wonder what this bill really has to do with the acquisition of power. Let me cite an example and in this way perhaps throw some light on the message of my western colleagues. Let me caution the Premiers of the provinces west of the Manitoba-Ontario border. Inherent in this piece of legislation is an uncontrolled de-

sire to effect total and absolute power, not in a wider and broader cabinet but in the hands of relatively few people. I wonder why the government and those close to it desire the type of power included in this legislation.
I refer to an article which appeared in a periodical in that city across the harbour from mine, the capital of Nova Scotia. It is entitled "The 4th Estate". In volume No. 2, issue No. 28, dated January 21, 1971-just eight or nine days ago-there is the headline, "Tom Kent Killing Maritimes". It is the use of power in such a manner that I have alluded to which would cause a reporter such as Dulcie Conrad, who has eight or ten years' experience in covering the political scene in Nova Scotia, to write the type of article the editor would feel deserved such a headline. Whether I am right or wrong, I have no pathological fear of Tom Kent, deputy minister notwithstanding. One must take note of such an article by a responsible reporter with some prestige and some ability, depending on whether you agree with her or are in favour of what she says at a given time.
I would like to quote from this article so as to demonstrate what I am afraid is really happening. I refer to the divide and conquer policy which a handful of people with tremendous power can apply. Miss Conrad writes:
The latest example of Mr. Kent's power over maritime planning was his order to Liberal Premier Gerald Regan of Nova Scotia to get rid of the province's newly formed cabinet secretariat, a planning body set up by the previous Conservative government. The secretariat had been making at least a tentative start at planning for Nova Scotia at the provincial level keeping in mind special provincial conditions and, hopefully, the feelings of the province's people.
What concerns me is that a perceptive writer would attempt to deal with power in this way. I do not believe that she is shooting down Tom Kent. I do not think Dulcie Conrad has a pathological fear of Tom Kent. She is really asking what happens to a province when a minister is given virtually unlimited authority to do things. What happened to Prince Edward Island? My dear friend and colleague, the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), is not here. If he were, he would tell you-and so would the people of P.E.I.-that they have lost their provincial rights, they have lost their autonomy.
I would not be afraid to bet a buck with anybody that in the preparation of budget considerations and papers for the forthcoming fiscal year, every blessed minister in that province had to submit them to Tom Kent for approval before they could come up with their final budget or estimates. The suggestion, of course, is that Tom Kent or the Deputy Minister of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is using the same type of control and the same type of power in the province of Nova Scotia. I am afraid of that type of power. I am afraid of a philosophy of political office that says: Let us appoint a whole lot of ministers. Let us so divide and conquer, let us so spread out the responsibility of government that any one of the responsible ministers can be ticked off just like that.
Government Organization Act, 1970
I am afraid of that. Better a powerful, single, bad man whom you can understand than the weakness that comes with the division of broad responsibilities so that surreptitious methods can be employed to usurp power, to take away power, and in this case to take away power from provinces which enjoy it and have every right to it.
The story is that Tom Kent is killing the Maritimes. By God, he had better not try it! But that is not all. So extensive is the article that the newspaper decided to editorialize it. The title reads, "Stop the Sellout to Ottawa". Again, this type of headline by an editor or an editorial writer is born out of a sense of fear, not of what could happen but what indeed is happening. Of course, the bill speeds up that process. It creates a ministry with tremendously broad authority and unlimited power which, mind you, is still open and above board. People can see and understand it and they can deal with what they can see and understand. But there is fear of a broadening of power, for whatever reason, of ministries about which we know nothing and whose authority is open-ended and unlimited. The author of the editorial asks:
Who should have the final say about how the three maritime provinces plan for their future future economic development?
This is a rhetorical question. There is no question about it in my mind. It has to be done jointly. That may surprise hon. members. It must be above board and open. But the intitiative and final authority must come from the Maritimes. The author goes on to answer the question, also rhetorically:
The federal government, which provides the bulk of the money for this development? Or the political leaders of the three provinces who are-or should be-in touch with what the people they serve feel are the important issues of development?
There's the old saying, he who pays the piper calls the tune.
It is this hidden uncertainty, this unknown quantity that gets me to my feet tonight to express some concern. I do not think the government is moving in this direction simply to create and enhance income positions for 60, 70, 80 or 100 of its members. I do not think they are quite that stupid. I do not believe they are quite so unsubtle as that. I think there is a much more sinister reason behind their action. There might not be, mind you, but I would still like to see a minister rise to his feet and talk seriously about what really is intended by this legislation and tell us what it means. What does the government intend to do with an unlimited number of ministries?
A colleague of mine on this side of the House said the other day that if they are interested in an efficient government there are many examples around the world at which they could look, not the least of which is the British House of Commons where with a relative handful of men-12 or so-they manage the affairs of a nation of 50 million or 60 million people. Great Britain has a unitary form of government. I wonder if that is what this government is after. I wonder sometimes whether they are trying to create such a proliferation of ministries that, for example, cities will rapidly become less concerned with dealing with Ottawa through their provincial legislatures. I wonder if this is what they are after.

The N.S. secretariat, and its chairman, planner Len Poestchke, are being axed by the provincial government because they could prove a thorn in the side of Mr. Regan when he wants to collect a fast bunch of goodies (in the form of money from Mr. Kent's Department of Regional Economic Expansion for such things as highways and sewerage systems).

The new Premier of the province of New Brunswick, Mr. Hatfield, hopefully has seen enough to know how to approach the federal authorities.

They do not know how much money they will be allowed to keep. They do not know whether a government directive will take money from them, money that will be used for purposes over which they have no control.
I think it is clear that the private sector of the country lack confidence in the immediate future. Such people are holding back. The last budget was an example of the government's philosophy. It would not cut taxes and allow citizens to decide how to spend their money. It kept taxes high and directed the money where it thought the funds would do most good. Evidently the government does not have the answers. We heard today that only about $40 million, or 25 per cent of the loan fund, has been taken up. Even that money will not work to create jobs. We also see that the government is doing its best to fill the gap left by private capital which has been leaving Quebec. I suggest that no government can fill a gap of that size.
In the meantime, those areas that could be productive, in the short term, in the creation of employment are not being attended to. Obviously the government does not know what to do. It does not have the right answers to our difficulties and as a result the economy is stagnating.

speechtext:
I do not know that they are saving it. Certainly they are spending it and even that does not seem to be doing any good. That course will never produce the results the government hopes to achieve. If the government has any desire to reorganize, I suggest it should begin at the bottom and not at the top. Let it begin with those areas that directly affect the private citizen. The private citizen is not overly concerned about the number of departments of government or ministers of state, except to the extent that the additional bodies will mean more expenditures and additional bureaucracies which grow under new ministers.
Although the concept of a department of the environment is good, I do not think much can be said for the rest of the bill. Before resuming my seat I would mention the superannuations dealt with in this bill. It appears to me that some of our senior civil servants were involved in the drafting of that part of the bill for their own benefit. I really do not see what merit there is in that portion of the legislation. What has this to do with a bill on government organization? I think that part of the bill should receive more attention from Your Honour. Your Honour ought to decide whether it is proper to include such a provision in this type of bill.

maintopic: NO TO AFFLUENCE IS THE PRICE OF POLLUTION CONTROL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as stated by several hon. members, a bill of this nature provides a tremendous amount of scope for debate because it encompasses so many aspects. I hear the government whip muttering from his seat. Regretfully, I did not hear what he said-not that it matters a great deal. Initially I wish to deal with that part of the bill which relates to the establishment of a department of the environment. I also have some views regarding other parts of the bill. As there are only five or six minutes remaining this evening, I will deal only briefly with the proposal to establish a department of the environment.
In recent years almost everyone has got into the act of pollution control. There has been a tremendous amount of discussion on the subject. A large number of community groups and organizations of a voluntary nature have become concerned with the environment and its quality and preservation. Politicians are not excluded from this exhibition of concern. At least on paper, the proposal of the government indicates that it wants to exhibit another aspect of its concern about environmental matters. Perhaps the most helpful aspect of concern which the general public is showing is the intensity with which the younger generation is approaching the problem. I am familiar with a great many grade school students in my constituency and other areas. Many of them have embarked upon essays and projects relating to environmental matters in their own areas. Some have even effected prosecutions against industries in contravention of the various provincial laws relating to pollution control. This is very gratifying because these young people

depend upon the heritage which we will establish. Young people feel they are going to live forever. There is a tremendous period of time in front of them. As one gets older, that period of time shortens. Perhaps that is why older people have a less enthusiastic and intense approach toward matters such as this.
The government is faced with the British North America Act. The government has not shown any great interest or desire in overcoming the problem of our Constitution. The British North America Act gives the provinces exclusive jurisdiction over matters relating to civil and property rights. The exercise of that jurisdiction prevents Parliament enacting legislation for environmental control or legislation that impinges upon the rights of provinces, municipalities and individuals. The Canada Water Act was passed in the last session of Parliament. It conceived establishing authorities and criteria for water quality control in Canada. The proposals in the Canada Water Act were, and still are, merely pious expressions. The act is of no value to Canadians unless there is mutual agreement with the provinces. As a consequence, we have a piecemeal approach to that aspect of the environment which relates to water.
The bill before us seeks to establish a department of the environment. Any companion legislation dealing with pollution of land, air or any other aspect of our environment will hinge upon agreement being worked out with the province. This does not apply to fisheries and shipping, where we have constitutional jurisdiction. That is not the proper approach to the matter. It simply reflects an oversensitivity on the part of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with regard to technical concepts and constitutional rights.
I am not suggesting that Parliament should take action which would override the constitutional authority of the provinces. Ethically and morally that is not right. In any event, it would flounder in the Supreme Court. The government is not prohibited from proposing to the provinces specific constitutional amendments to deal with the environment. In 1941 there was an amendment which dealt with unemployment insurance. A few years ago there was a constitutional amendment dealing with survivors benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. At that time there was unanimous agreement on the part of the provinces to give this authority to Parliament.
The matter of environmental control is as vital as life itself. If we do not act quickly, there may only be two or three generations of life left in the world. Surely this fact should be important enough for the government to overcome its extreme sensitivity about the constitutional question and directly propose to the provinces that differences of opinion about the Constitution be set aside. Surely there is some common ground where Parliament can have jurisdiction over environmental matters. Rather than approach the subject on a piecemeal basis by agreement with the provinces, it should be dealt with by Parliament because the problem is national in scope.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-DISCONTINUANCE OF DINING CAR SERVICE. OTTAWA-MONTREAL
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-DISCONTINUANCE OF DINING CAR SERVICE. OTTAWA-MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some time ago Canadian National Railways announced it was going to discontinue the dining car service on their passenger trains between Montreal and Ottawa. When the CNR made that announcement, several of us in this House protested. I personally approached the president of the CNR, the president of the Canadian Transport Commission and the minister. Hon. members protested because, to begin with, these trains travel at the breakfast hour and the supper hour and have been receiving very heavy patronage. As a matter of fact, I travel on these trains very often and it is not uncommon for me to have to wait up to half an hour before I can get into the dining car.
In addition, many people use this train between Ottawa and Montreal-a service between the national capital and Canada's metropolis-because the highway is so bad that it is almost impossible to drive upon it safely. I think someone wrote an article recently pointing out that this stretch of highway has had the highest rate of accidents and deaths in Canada for the last few years. We based our protest also on the fact that more people would be put out of work at this time of heavy unemployment if this service were withdrawn.
In posing my question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson] last Friday, I asked whether he had received any further answer from the CNR on this matter and he replied he had not. At that time I had not received any answer from the CNR either, but today I received an answer from the president of the CNR in which he stated that despite the use of the service, the CNR is sustaining a loss of $300,000 annually. I am not suggesting that the government of Canada should subsidize people's meals on this service to the tune of $300,000 a year. But I am wondering whether the railway has really looked into alternate methods of providing dining car service. I think many people would be willing to pay

an additional amount to receive a good meal in the morning and at supper time. Has the company investigated the possibility of giving out a concession for this service?
What really disturbs me is this. I support what has been said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I was a member of the transport committee which put forward the report on pensions, and what bothers me is the way the CNR disregards the wishes of the elected representatives of the people. It seems to me that the CNR should not only administer this national railway in an economical and efficient manner, but should also administer it with a social conscience. I am not convinced that they do this. They are not doing this with respect to pension plans, they are not doing it when they take off a dining car service at a time like this.
The minister's representative is here tonight, and through him I ask the CNR to reconsider this whole decision. I ask them to reconsider whether there might not be a way of providing this service and in particular I ask them to pay more attention to the fact that they are a national railway. They should serve the needs of Canadian people. When they come here from time to time and ask for money through a finance bill, we should have the right, as members of Parliament did in the seventeenth century in England, to refuse them money until they deal with our grievances.
